(Surah Ta-Ha is Meccan, except verses 130 and 131, which are Medinan; its verses number 135.)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ta-Ha.﴾ Qalun, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Hafs and Ya'qub pronounced both letters with fatha (the 'original' reading). Abu 'Amr alone pronounced the ta' with fatha, while Warsh did so because of its emphatic (isti'la') quality, and the rest (al-Baqun) pronounced both with imala (inclination). It is one of the disjointed letters (al-fawatih) with which the noble surahs begin, and this is the view of the majority of the precise scholars (al-mutqinin). It has also been said that its meaning is: "O man" (ya rajul). This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and from al-Hasan, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, 'Ikrimah and al-Kalbi, except that according to Sa'id it is in the Nabataean language, according to Qatadah in Syriac, according to 'Ikrimah in Abyssinian, and according to al-Kalbi in the dialect of 'Aka, said to be 'Ukl, which is a Yemeni dialect. They said: If this is authentic, then perhaps its original form is ya ha dha (O this man), and they altered it by changing the ya' into ta' and dropping dha from ha dha. As for what is cited from the verse of the poet:

"Indeed, folly, Ta-Ha, is among your dispositions; may Allah not sanctify the characters of the accursed."

this is not a clear proof for that, since it may be an oath, as in the case of Ha-Mim ﴿they will not be helped﴾. It has also been permitted that the original form is ta'ha, an imperative from wata'a (to tread), so that the hamza in yata'u was changed to an alif because of the opening before it, as in the saying of one who said: "There is no pasture there (la hunaka al-mar'a)", and ha is a pronoun referring to the earth, on the basis that it is an address to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to tread the earth with his feet, since he used to stand in his night prayer on one leg, out of exaggeration in striving. But this is rejected by their being written in the form of the letters, just as interpreting it as "O man" is rejected, since writing them in the shapes of letters while pronouncing them otherwise is a characteristic of the letters of the alphabet. It has also been read as "Taha", either on the basis that its original form is ta', whose hamza was changed to ha as in words like hараqat (she spilled), or the hamza in yata'u was changed to an alif as mentioned, and then the imperative was formed from it with the silent ha (ha al-sakt) attached. Or it is on the basis that it suffices in pronunciation with the two halves of the two names, and these halves are placed in the position of the names in indicating the named entities, so that they are as if they were the names that indicate them. On this basis the saying of the one who said should be understood. Or it suffices with the halves of the two words and refers to them by their names; otherwise the two halves are not mentioned in the sense that they are named by their names so as to serve as expressions of them, but rather in the sense that they are parts of them, which is sufficient in mentioning them instead of mentioning them; therefore the pronunciation fell upon the halves themselves and not upon their names, by taking the dual pronoun in both places to refer to the halves insofar as they are named, and not insofar as they are parts of the names; and the intended meaning of "their name" is the halves insofar as they stand in place of the names. The meaning, then, is that in pronunciation it suffices with the halves of the two words, i.e., the two names, so it refers to them, i.e., the halves, insofar as they are named by them, insofar as they stand in place of the names. As for interpreting it to mean that in writing it suffices with the halves of the two words, meaning ta' on the assumption that it is an imperative and that it is a vocative particle, and ha on the assumption that it is a pronoun for the earth and that it is an interjection of alerting, and that one departed from those two halves in pronouncing their names, this is clearly invalid, since the ta' and ha, according to the assumed possibilities mentioned, are not names for the two letters mentioned; rather the first is an imperative or a vocative particle, and the second is a pronoun for the earth or an interjection of alerting. Moreover, writing the form of the letter and pronouncing it otherwise is a characteristic of the letters of the alphabet, as already mentioned. Therefore the truth is what has preceded: that they are among the disjointed letters, either recited in the pattern of enumeration in one of the two ways mentioned at the beginning of (Surat al-Baqarah), in which case they have no grammatical position (mahall min al-i'rab).

And likewise what follows them, from His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 2:

﴿We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you should be distressed.﴾ This is a resumed statement (isti'naf) brought to console him (ﷺ) for the hardship (ta'ab) he suffered from the polytheists, for distress (shaqa') is common in that sense. From it comes the saying: "More distressed than a colt's trainer" (ashqa min ra'id muhr). That is: We did not send it down upon you that you should exhaust yourself by exaggerating in enduring hardships, in disputing with the obstinate and arguing with the tyrants, and in excessive grief over their disbelief in it, and anguish that they do not believe, as in His saying, mighty and majestic is He, to him: ﴿Perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief over their footsteps...﴾ to the end of the verse. Rather, it is for conveying and reminding, and you have done so; so there is no blame upon you if they do not believe after that. Or it is to turn him (ﷺ) away from his excessive striving in worship, as it is narrated that "he (ﷺ) used to stand in prayer at night until his feet swelled, and Jibril (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Spare yourself, for your self has a right over you.'" That is: We did not send it down upon you that you should exhaust yourself by wearing down your soul and compelling it to severe exercises and crushing hardships; you were sent only with the tolerant, easy monotheism (al-hanifiyya al-samhah).

It is said that Abu Jahl and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "You are wretched, since you have abandoned the religion of your fathers, and the Qur'an was sent down to you so that you would be wretched by it." So He refuted that by saying: "We did not send it down upon you as they claimed." The first interpretation is the most suitable, as the following exception (al-istithna' al-ati) testifies.

As for "Ta-Ha" (ṭā hā), it may be a noun for the Qur'an, its place being in the nominative case, as the subject (mubtada'), with what follows it as its predicate (khabar), and "al-Qur'an" being an apparent noun placed in the position of the pronoun returning to the subject, as if it were said: "The Qur'an, We did not send it down upon you that you should be distressed." Or it is in the accusative by supposing an oath verb, or in the genitive by estimating its particle, and what follows is its answer.

On these two readings it is also permissible for it to be a name for the surah, unlike the first reading, for on that assumption it does not work out; yet not because the subject would then remain without a returning pronoun or a substitute for it, since the Qur'an certainly applies to the surah, either by way of identity, in that what is meant is the common notion shared by the whole and the part, or by way of inclusion if what is meant is the whole. Rather, it is because negating that its sending down is for distress requires that distress had already occurred as a consequence of its sending down, definitely, either in reality, as when what is meant is the meaning of hardship, or according to the claim of the disbelievers, as when what is meant is the opposite of happiness. There is no doubt that this is conceivable only in the sending down of what was sent down previously; but the sending down of the noble surah is not something by which the prior distress could be consequent, so as to be disposed to negate it from it. As for the aspect of identity, it is evident; and as for the aspect of inclusion, its implication is that it be said: "This surah: We did not send down the Qur'an containing it that you should be distressed," and it is not hidden that making it the thing reported about, although the sending down of it has no bearing whatsoever on the prior distress, is not befitting to the dignity of the glorious revelation.

The words ﴿except as a reminder﴾ are in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu, the accusative of purpose) governing "We sent down." However, this is not because the reminder is motivated by the hardship, in the sense that the meaning is: We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would exhaust yourself in conveying it, except as a reminder, and so on. This is like your saying: "I did not strike you for discipline, except out of compassion," because in such examples there must be a connection of causality and effect between the two motives, as in the example given. And in your saying: "I did not rebuke you harshly so that you would be hurt, except to deter others," the discipline in the first case is caused by compassion, and the being hurt in the second is a cause of deterring others. You already know the contradiction between hardship and reminder, and it is of no use to take the hardship here to mean general toil that includes the reminder, because it is evident that there is no connection between them of the causal kind mentioned. That could only be conceived if it were said in place of ﴿except as a reminder﴾: "except to multiply your reward," since the reward is proportionate to the toil. Nor is it because it is a substitute (badal, substitution or apposition) for the position of ﴿so that you would be distressed﴾, as in His words: ﴿They did not do it, except a few﴾, because the two substitutes must be of the same kind, and you know their状态 (situation) in this regard. Rather, it is because it is conjoined to that in meaning, after its negation, by way of correction (istidrak, a corrective contrast) derived from a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', an exception not of the same category as what precedes), as if it were said: We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would exhaust yourself in conveying it, but rather as a reminder ﴿for those who fear﴾. The reminder has been stripped of the preposition lam because it is an act of the doer of the motivated verb, i.e., for those whose nature it is to fear God, the Mighty and Exalted, and to be affected by warning because of the tenderness of their hearts and the softness of their disposition; or for those whom God, may He be exalted, knows will fear through intimidation. The specification of them, despite the generality of the reminder and conveyance, is because they are the ones who benefit from it.

And His saying, ﴿a revelation﴾ (*tanzilan*), is a verbal noun (*masdar*) emphasizing an implied verb in a resumptive sentence that confirms what precedes it, meaning: "It was sent down as a revelation." Or it emphasizes what the exceptive clause (*al-jumla al-istithna'iyya*) implies, since it contains the sense of saying, "We sent it down as a reminder." The first is more suitable to what follows of the shift in person (*iltifat*). Or it is in the accusative of praise and specification. It has also been said that it is in the accusative as the object of ﴿fears﴾ (*yakhsha*), meaning: "He fears a revelation from Allah, exalted is He." You know that linking fear and dread and similar things to revelation in general is not customary. Yes, such fear may be linked to some parts of it that contain threats and similar matters, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down about them, informing them of what is in their hearts﴾.

It has also been said that it is a substitute (*badal*) for *tadhkira* (reminder), but not on the basis that it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*) for *anzalna* (We sent down), since a thing cannot be explained by itself or by its kind. Rather, it is on the basis that it is a verbal noun in the sense of the active participle, standing in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the *kaf* in ʿalayka (upon you), or from the Qur'an. It has no acceptable standing except as a qualifier of *anzalna*, after its qualification by the first qualifier, and you have already learned its status in what preceded.

It has been read as *tanzilun* (a revelation), as the predicate of an omitted subject.

The *man* in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from the One who created the earth and the high heavens﴾ is connected to *tanzilan*, or to an implied verb that is a qualifier of it, confirming through its specificity the inherent grandeur of its indefinite form with relational grandeur. The attribution of the revelation to the relative pronoun comes by way of shifting to the third person after its attribution to the nun of majesty (*nun al-'azama*), to show His exalted grandeur in terms of acts and attributes, following its demonstration in terms of essence in a vague manner. Then comes the explanation for further confirmation and establishment, and the specification of the creation of these two by mention, although what is meant is the creation of both together with all that is connected to them, as His saying, exalted is He, makes clear: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth﴾, and so on, because these two are primary and everything else follows them. The earth is placed first because it is closer to the senses and more evident to them. He described the heavens with *al-ʿula*, which is the plural of *al-ʿulya*, the feminine of *al-a'la* (highest), to emphasize grandeur, together with what it contains of regard for the verse endings (*fawasil*). All of this, up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾, is directed toward magnifying the status of the One who sends down, exalted and majestic is He, and of what is sent down, which calls for the nurturing of humility and the inducing of awe that leads to bringing down those who rebel from the rank of arrogance and transgression, and attracts them toward the fear that leads to remembrance and faith.

The Most Merciful (﴿الرَّحْمَنُ﴾) is in the nominative case by way of praise (al-madh), meaning: He is the Most Merciful. You have already learned at the beginning of (Surat al-Baqarah) that a noun in the nominative for praise has the status of a descriptive qualifier (sifah) relating to what precedes it, even though it does not follow it in i'rab (grammatical case). For this reason they required omitting the subject (mubtada') so that it takes the form of one of the complements of that subject. (p-5) It has also been read in the genitive, as a plain descriptive qualifier of the relative pronoun. What is said, that incomplete names (al-asma' al-naqisah) may only be described by the one who is singular, is the position of the Kufan grammarians. In any case, describing Him with mercy right after describing Him as the Creator of the heavens and the earth serves to indicate that their creation is among the effects of His mercy, exalted is He. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, the Most Merciful﴾, is to announce that His lordship is by way of mercy. It also contains an indication that the sending down of the Qur'an is likewise among the rulings of His mercy, exalted is He, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿The Most Merciful, taught the Qur'an﴾. Or it is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), with the definite article (al-lam) indicating a known reference, the pointing is to the relative pronoun, and the predicate is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He settled upon the Throne﴾. Mercy has been made the heading of the topic, whose nature is that its attribution to the topic should be known to the addressee, to announce that this is a clear matter, not concealed, and independent of being stated explicitly. "Upon" (ʿalā) is related to "settled" (istawā) and was placed before it for the sake of observing the verse endings (fawasil). The prepositional phrase, according to the first view, is the predicate of an omitted subject, as in the genitive reading. It has also been permitted that it be a predicate following a predicate.

Settling upon the Throne (al-istiwa' ʿala al-ʿarsh) is a figurative expression (majaz) for sovereignty and rule, derived from the allusion (kinayah) regarding one who is permitted to sit upon a couch. It is said: so-and-so settled upon the throne of kingship, meaning he became king, even if he did not sit upon the couch at all. The intended meaning is to clarify the connection of His noble will to the bringing into existence of beings and the management of their affairs.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, whether that belonging is by way of being a part of them, in whatever sense that may be, or by indwelling in them.

﴿And what is between them﴾ of the existent things that are in the air constantly, such as the air and the clouds, or more so, such as the birds; that is, He alone, not any other, without partnership and without independence, possesses all that has been mentioned, in ownership, disposal, giving life, causing to incline, bringing into existence, and bringing to nonexistence.

﴿And what is beneath the soil﴾, that is, what lies beyond the dust. Its mention, although it falls under what is in the earth, is for the sake of added emphasis. It is narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b that it refers to what is beneath the seven earths. And it is narrated from al-Suddi that al-Thara is the rock upon which the seventh earth rests.

And if you speak aloud, [He knows it]. This is an explanation of the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of all things, following the explanation of the vastness of His dominion and the all-encompassing scope of His power over all beings. That is: and if you raise your voice in mentioning Him, may He be exalted, and in supplicating to Him, then know that He, may He be exalted, is free of need of your loudness.

Indeed He knows the secret and what is more hidden. That is, what you confide to another, and something more hidden than that, namely what you bring to mind without uttering it at all; or what you confide to yourself, and what is more hidden than that, namely what you will confide in the future. Its indefiniteness (in "shay'an," "something") is for emphasis on hiddenness. This is either a prohibition against loud speech, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And mention your Lord within yourself, humbly and in fear, and without loud speech﴾, or a guidance for the servants, except that loudness is not for His hearing, may He be glorified, but for another purpose: impressing the remembrance upon the soul and fixing it therein, preventing it from occupation with other things, cutting off whispering from it, and subduing it through humility and supplication.

"Allah" is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is a resumptive clause (istinaf) brought to show that the one described by the attributes of perfection mentioned is that deity, the Truly Worshipped, i.e., that the one characterized by the sublime qualities mentioned is Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is no deity except Him﴾, is an affirmation of the truth and an explicit statement of what the preceding context implied, namely that divinity (uluhiyyah) belongs exclusively to Him, glory be to Him. For what is ascribed to Him, Exalted is He, of creating all existing things, (p-6) of being the Most Merciful (al-Rahmaniyyah), of being the Owner of all, and of comprehensive knowledge, clearly requires it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾, is an explanation that what has been mentioned of creation, mercy (al-Rahmaniyyah), ownership, and being Lord of the worlds (al-'Alamiyyah) are His names and attributes, without any plurality in His essence, Exalted is He. It is related that when the polytheists heard the Prophet ﷺ saying, "O Allah, O Most Merciful," they said: "He forbids us to worship two gods, yet he calls upon another god." Al-husna (the most beautiful) is the feminine form of al-ahsan (the most beautiful), which is used as an adjective for a feminine singular; the plural of the masculine and feminine is used likewise, as in ﴿maarib ukhra﴾ (other uses) and ﴿aayaatina al-kubra﴾ (Our greatest signs).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 9:

﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ This is a resumptive statement (istinaf), brought in to establish the matter of Tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), to which the thread of the narrative ultimately leads, and to show that this matter has been continuous among the prophets, one great figure after another. It was addressed to Moses, peace be upon him, when it was said to him: ﴿Indeed, I am God; there is no god but Me﴾, and with it he, peace be upon him, concluded his own speech when he said: ﴿Your god is only God, besides whom there is no god﴾. As for what has been said, that this was meant to encourage the Prophet ﷺ to follow the example of Moses, peace be upon him, in bearing the burdens of prophethood and patiently enduring the hardships of conveying the rulings of the message, this is rejected by the fact that the context of the noble discourse is directed at turning him, peace be upon him, away from plunging into difficulties.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary on surah 20, verse 10 (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When he saw a fire﴾ is an adverbial complement (ẓarf) governing "the narration." It has been said that it governs an implied verb placed after it, meaning: when he saw a fire, such-and-such happened. It has also been said that it is an object of an implied verb placed before it, meaning: remember the time he saw a fire.

It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, asked Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both, for permission to leave to go to his mother and his brother. He left with his family and took a route other than the usual one, fearing the kings of Syria. When he reached the valley of Tuwa, which lies on the western side of Mount Sinai (al-Tur), a son was born to him on a dark, wintry, icy night. It was a Friday night. He had lost his way, his livestock had scattered, and he had no water. He struck (his flint) to make fire, but his spark failed. While he was in this state, he saw a fire on the left side of the road, on the side of the mountain. ﴿So he said to his family: "Stay here"﴾, that is, remain where you are. He, peace be upon him, ordered them to do this so that they would not follow him in his intention to go to the fire, as was customary, and not so that they would move to another place, for that did not occur to him. The address is to the wife, the child and the servant. It has been said that it was addressed to her alone. The plural form is either because of the outward wording "family" (ahl), or for emphasis, as in the words of the one who said: [And if you wish, I will forbid women other than you].

﴿Indeed I have perceived a fire﴾, that is, I have seen it with clear sight, with no doubt about it. It has been said that "perceiving" (iyns) is specific to seeing what brings comfort. The clause is a justification for the command or for what was commanded.

﴿Perhaps I may bring you from it﴾, that is, I may come to you from the fire.

﴿A brand﴾, that is, a burning torch taken from the main body of the fire. This is what is meant by the "brand" (jadhwa) in (Surah al-Qasas) and by the "flame" (shihab) as "qabas."

﴿Or find at the fire guidance﴾, a guide who will show me the way. This is either a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as a name for the agent for emphasis, or an attribute whose governed noun has been omitted, meaning: one possessing guidance. Or it means that when the guide is found, guidance has been found. It has been said: a guide who will lead me to the gates of religion, for the thoughts of the righteous are immersed in religious concern throughout their circumstances, and no distraction turns them from it. The first interpretation is more apparent, because the context of the noble verse is to console his family. This is explicitly stated in (Surah al-Qasas), where it is said: ﴿Perhaps I may bring you from it news or a brand﴾, and so on. The word "or" in both places denotes permissibility of the absence of both, not prohibition of combining them.

The meaning of elevation in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿at the fire﴾ is that the people of the fire ascend the place near it, or that when they warm themselves they surround it standing and sitting, so they overlook it. Since bringing the two was expected and not certain to occur, he began the clause with the word of hope ("perhaps"). It is either a cause for an omitted verb, relied upon because of what indicates it from the command to remain and the report of the fire's comforting presence, and to avoid explicitly stating what would frighten them; or it is a circumstantial clause for its subject, meaning: "So I go to it in order to come to you," or "so that I may come to you," or "hoping that I may come to you from it with a brand," and so on. The verification of this has been discussed in detail in the commentary on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous﴾ (Qur'an 2:21).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 11:

﴿When he came to it﴾, that is, the fire that he had perceived. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: He saw a green tree, around which, from its bottom to its top, there was a white fire blazing in the brightest manner possible, so he stood amazed at the intensity of its light and the intensity of the tree's greenness. The fire did not alter its greenness, and the abundance of the tree's water did not alter its light.

They said: Fire is of four kinds. One kind eats but does not drink, and this is the fire of this world. Another kind drinks but does not eat, and this is the fire of the green tree. A third kind eats and drinks, and this is the fire of Jahannam. A fourth kind neither eats nor drinks, and this is the fire of Musa, peace be upon him.

They also said: It is of four types. One type has light and burning, and this is the fire of this world. One type has neither light nor burning, and this is the fire of trees. One type has light without burning, and this is the fire of Musa, peace be upon him. And one type has burning without light, and this is the fire of Jahannam. It is narrated that the tree was a 'awsajah (a thorny shrub), and it was said that it was a samurah (a species of acacia).

﴿He was called: "O Musa"﴾, that is: he was called, and it was said: "O Musa."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 12:

﴿Indeed, I am your Lord﴾. Or the calling (al-nida') was treated as speech (qawl), since it is a form of it. It was also read with a fath (open vowel) on the hamza, meaning "that I am" (bi-anni). The repetition of the pronoun serves to emphasize the indication, to confirm the knowledge, and to remove doubt. It is narrated that when he was called, "O Musa," upon him be peace, said: "Who is speaking?" Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "I am your Lord." Then Iblis whispered to him: "Perhaps you are hearing the speech of a devil." He said: "I know that it is the speech of Allah, Exalted, because I hear it from all directions, with all the limbs." I say: this is because hearing what is not, by its nature, heard through those limbs is nothing but an effect of the power of the Creator, the All-Knowing, Exalted and Sanctified be He. It has also been said that upon him be peace received the speech of the Lord of Might through a spiritual reception (talaqqi ruhani), then that speech took the form of a body for him and passed into the common sense (al-hiss al-mushtarak, the faculty that unifies the senses), and was impressed upon him without being confined to one organ of his face.

﴿So take off your sandals﴾. Upon him be peace was commanded to do this, because going barefoot is more conducive to humility and good manners. For this reason the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-salih) used to circumambulate the Ka'ba barefoot. It has been said: so that he would touch the valley with his feet, seeking blessing through it. It has also been said: because his sandals were made of the skin of an undressed donkey. And it has been said: its meaning is, empty your heart of family and wealth. The fa' (so) indicates the ordering of the command upon what precedes it, for His Lordship over him, upon him be peace, is among the causes and motives of the command. His saying, Exalted be He, ﴿Indeed, you are in the sacred valley﴾ is the reason for the obligation of the removal commanded, and an explanation of the cause for the command, namely the nobility and sanctity of the place. It is narrated that upon him be peace removed them and threw them behind the valley.

﴿Tuwa﴾ with a damma on the ta' (ṭ), not nunated (ghayr munawwan). It was also read nunated, and read with a kasra, both nunated and not nunated. Whoever read it nunated interpreted it as a place (al-makan) rather than an area (al-buq'a). It has been said that it is like thuna from al-tayy (folding), a verbal noun (maṣdar) either of "he was called" (nuwdiya), meaning he was called twice, or of "the sacred" (al-muqaddas), meaning he was sanctified once after another.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 13:

﴿And I have chosen you﴾. That is: I have selected you (istafaytuka) for prophethood (nubuwwah) and messengership (risalah). It is also read: "Wa-inna khtarnaka" (﴿And indeed We have chosen you﴾), with both fath and kasr on the hamza of inna. The fa' in His words ﴿so listen﴾ indicates the connection of the command, or of the thing commanded, to what precedes it, since His choosing him, peace be upon him, for what has been mentioned is among the things that necessitate listening and the command to listen. The lam in His words, exalted is He, ﴿to what is revealed﴾ is connected to "listen" (istama'), and "ma" is either a relative pronoun (mawsulah) or a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), meaning: listen to that which is revealed to you, or to the revelation itself, not connected to "I have chosen you" as has been said. However, it is not connected in the manner that has been said, since that is from the category of tanazu' (competition between two verbs over one complement) and i'mal al-awwal (giving priority to the first verb).

Therefore it is necessary, in that case, to repeat the pronoun with the second item. Rather, [the reason is that] His saying, ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me﴾, is an apposition (badal) for "what is revealed." There is no doubt that His choosing him, peace and blessings be upon him, is not for this revelation alone. The "fa" in His saying, ﴿so worship Me﴾, indicates the sequencing of the command upon what precedes it, for the exclusivity of divinity (uluhiyyah) to Him, glorified and exalted, is among the requirements of restricting worship to Him, mighty and majestic.

﴿And establish prayer﴾. Prayer is singled out for mention and is given a separate command, although it is included in the command to worship, because of its virtue and its elevated status above the other acts of worship, since it is bound up with the remembrance of the Worshipped and with occupying the heart and tongue with His remembrance. This is His saying, ﴿for My remembrance﴾, that is: so that you may remember Me. For My remembrance, as it should be, is realized only within worship and prayer; or [it means] so that you remember Me within it, since it includes the invocations (adhkar); or [it means] for the remembrance of Me specifically, not mixed with the remembrance of other than Me; or [it means] for the sincere remembrance of Me and seeking My countenance, not showing off with it and not intending by it any other aim; or [it means] so that you are one who remembers Me without forgetting. It has also been said: [it means] for My remembering it and My commanding it in the Books; or so that I may mention you with praise and commendation. It has also been said: [it means] for the times of My remembrance, which are the times of the prayer; or for the remembrance of My prayer, based on what is narrated that he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers it, for Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾." And it was read: "li-dhikrā" with the feminine alif (ذكرى), and "lil-dhikrā" as a definite form, and "lil-dhikr" with definite and indefinite readings.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 15:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾ is a reason (ta'līl) for the obligation of worship and the establishment of prayer, meaning: it is certainly going to occur. It was expressed by the word "coming" (ityān) to affirm its realization, by presenting it in the form of a matter that is certain and directed toward the addressees.

﴿I almost conceal it﴾ means: I do not reveal it, by saying that it is coming, were it not that what is in informing them of it contains gentleness (luṭf) and the removal of excuses for what you did. Or it means: I almost reveal it, by bringing about [the Hour] for the one whom one conceals (akhfāhu), when one reveals it by removing its concealment. This is supported by the reading with a fatḥah on the hamzah, from khafāhu, meaning: he revealed it. It has been said that akhfāhu belongs to the words with opposite meanings (aḍdād), coming to mean both revealing and concealing.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ is connected to "coming" (ātiyah), and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirāḍ), or it is connected to "I conceal it" according to the last meaning. The "mā" is a verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah), meaning: so that every soul may be recompensed for its striving in attaining what has been mentioned of the matters commanded. Specifying it within the context of the purpose (ghāyah) of its coming, although the recompense is for every soul according to what proceeds from it, whether it was striving toward what has been mentioned or entirely neglectful of it or striving to attain its opposite, is to signal that the principal aim of its coming is the reward for worship. As for punishment for abandoning it, it is among the consequences of the bad choice of the disobedient; and [this is also indicated by the fact] that the commanded matter is in the force of obligation, and the Hour is in such intensity of terror and awfulness that they necessitate upon every soul that it strive to comply with the command, and seek to attain what saves it from acts of obedience, and then it guards against committing what ruins it of acts of disobedience. Upon this turns the matter in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water, that He might test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾. For the trial, although it encompasses all the responsible (mukallafīn) in terms of their deeds, which are divided into good and bad, and not only into good and better, has nevertheless been linked to the latter two, because of what has been mentioned: that the primary purpose of originating those wonders in that marvelous pattern is the manifestation of the perfection of the goodness of the good-doers, and that this, being in the most complete of the pleasing aspects and the most perfect of the fitting modes, necessitates acting upon its requirement, such that no one deviates from its clear ways; rather, every individual is guided to what it directs toward of general faith and obedience, and the disparity among them lies only in their levels of these according to strength and weakness. As for turning away from that and falling into the abysses of error, it is far from occurring, let alone being included in the sequence of the purpose of that wondrous creation; it is rather a deed that proceeds from its doer through his bad choice, without any justification for it or warrant for this. It is also permissible that "striving" be understood as action in general.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 16:

﴿So let not one who does not believe in it turn you away from it, lest you perish﴾ That is: from remembrance of the Hour and from being mindful of it. It has also been said: from affirming it. The first is the more fitting for the situation of Musa, peace be upon him. Although the prohibition is by way of exciting and inciting, the placing of the prepositional phrase "from it" before His words, Exalted is He, ﴿who does not believe in it﴾, is for the reason repeatedly mentioned before: the emphasis on what is placed first and the arousing of anticipation for what is placed later. For what should be placed first, when it is postponed, leaves the soul looking forward to it, so that when it arrives it settles in with far greater firmness. Also, because the postponed element would have a kind of length which, if placed first, might impair the eloquence of the noble composition. And although this, on the surface, is a prohibition to the disbeliever from turning Musa, peace be upon him, away from the Hour, in reality it is a prohibition to him, peace be upon him, from being turned away from it, in the most eloquent and emphatic manner. For the prohibition of the causes of a thing and its beginnings that lead to it is a prohibition of it by demonstrative means, and an annulment of causation from its very root, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And let not the hatred of a people ...﴾ and so on, for the turning away of the disbeliever, inasmuch as it is the cause of his, peace be upon him, being turned away, the prohibition concerning it is a prohibition of its very origin and what necessitates it, and an annulment of it entirely. It is also permissible that it be of the category of prohibiting the effect while intending the prohibition of the cause, on the basis that what is intended is his, peace be upon him, being prohibited from showing gentleness toward the disbelievers, for that is a cause of their turning him away, peace be upon him, as in the saying: "I shall not find you here," where what is meant is the prohibition of the addressee from being present before him, which necessitates seeing him.

﴿And follows his desire﴾ That is: what his soul desires of sensual, transient pleasures.

﴿Then you will perish﴾ That is: then you will be destroyed. For neglecting it and neglecting the acquisition of what saves from its terrors necessarily entails destruction. It is in the accusative position as a response to the prohibition, or in the nominative position on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "then you are perishing."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 17:

﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?﴾ This begins the narration of what he (peace be upon him) was charged with concerning matters related to creation, following the narration of what he was commanded concerning matters specific to himself. So "ma" (what) is interrogative and in the position of the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and "tilka" (that) is its predicate (khabar), or the reverse, and the latter is more fitting in meaning and better suited to the answer. "Bi-yaminika" (in your right hand) is connected to an implied verb that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: "And what is that remaining in your right hand, or held in your right hand?" The governing element is the sense of pointing (al-ishara), as in His words, Mighty and Exalted, ﴿And this is my husband, an old man﴾. It has also been said: "tilka" is a relative pronoun, meaning: "What is it that is in your right hand?" In either case, the interrogation is an alert and a caution to him (peace be upon him) regarding the marvels that will appear to him. The repetition of the address (al-nida') is for added intimacy and attentiveness.

**"He said, 'It is my staff.'"** He attributed it to himself to affirm that it was in his right hand, and to prepare for the actions that follow, which are attributed to him, peace be upon him. It is read as **"ʿaṣayya"** (with the final vowel doubled), according to the dialect of the tribe of Hudhayl. **"I lean upon it"**, meaning I rely on it when I am weary or when I stand over the flock.

**"And I beat down [leaves] with it for my sheep."** That is, I strike the leaves with it and make them fall. It is also read **"ahishshu"** with a kasra on the *hāʾ*. Both forms derive from *hashsha al-khubzu yahishshu*, meaning the bread broke because of its brittleness. It is also read with an unpointed *sīn* (**"asussu"**), which is the driving of sheep. It takes **ʿalā** because the verb is construed with the meaning of "turning away from" and "turning toward," so the sense is: I drive them away, turning from them and toward them.

**"And I have other uses for it."** That is, other needs of this kind. Like what is reported: when he, peace be upon him, travelled, he would lay it across his shoulder and hang his belongings on it, such as the bow, the quiver, the milking vessel, and the like. When he was in the desert, he would plant it in the ground, spread his garments over its forked top, cast a cloth over it, and shade himself beneath it. When the rope was too short, he would join it to the staff. When wild beasts attacked his flock, he would fight them with it. It is also said that among its uses: it had two forks and a crook. When a branch was too long, he would bend it with the crook, and when he wished to break it, he would twist it with the two forks.

It seems that he, peace be upon him, understood that the purpose of the question was to explain its essence and to detail its benefits thoroughly. Then, when it appeared contrary to that essence and manifested wondrous properties, he knew that these were manifest signs and overpowering miracles that God Most High had brought about, and were not among the properties ordinarily resulting from it. So he mentioned its essence and benefits, both in detail and in summary, meaning that it is of the kind of staves, carrying with it the benefits of its fellow staves, so that his answer would correspond to the aim he understood from the question of the All-Knowing, the All-Aware.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 19:

﴿Qāla﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf), built upon a question that naturally arises in the mind, as if it were said: "Then what did He, Mighty and Majestic, say?" So it is answered: He said, ﴿Throw it down, O Musa﴾, so that you may see of its affair what has not occurred to your mind of matters. And the repetition of the address (al-nidā') is for emphasis of the alerting (li-ta'kīd al-tanbīh).

Then he threw it down on the ground, and behold, it was a snake moving swiftly. It was related that when he (peace be upon him) threw it, it turned into a snake, yellow in color and as thick as the staff. Then it swelled and grew large, and for this reason it was likened to the jann (the jinn-serpent) at one time, and was called a thu'ban (a large serpent) at another. Here the general term was used for both states. It was also said that it had turned into a thu'ban from the very beginning, and this is more fitting to the context, as His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He, reveals: ﴿Then behold, it was a manifest serpent﴾. It was likened to the jann only in its boldness and swiftness of movement, not in the smallness of its body. As for His saying, Exalted is He, "tas'a" (moving swiftly), it is either an adjective of ḥayyah (serpent), or a second predicate according to those who permit it to be a clause.

﴿قالَ﴾ (He said) is a resumptive clause (istinaf, a new sentence that answers an implied question), as before. ﴿خُذْها ولا تَخَفْ﴾ (Take it and do not fear). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: it turned into a male serpent that swallowed everything of the rocks and trees. When he saw it like that, he was frightened and fled, and what overcame him is what overcomes a human being when witnessing terrors and frightful things: fright and flight. The joining of the prohibition to the command (fi 'atf al-nahy 'ala al-amr) indicates that the absence of what is forbidden (al-mantahi 'anhu) is intended for its own sake, not merely to fulfil what is commanded. ﴿سَنُعِيدُها سِيرَتَها الأُولى﴾ (We shall return it to its original form). Although it is a resumptive clause directed to give the reason for complying with the command and the prohibition, its meaning, that We return it to what it was, which is among the requirements of taking it and of not fearing it, is a gracious promise, with the showing of another miracle at the outset of his mission, peace be upon him, and an announcement that it is subjected to his command, so that he would be at peace concerning his affair and no trace of wavering would affect him when disputing with Pharaoh. That is: We shall return it after taking it to its first state, which is the form of a staff (al-hay'ah al-'asawiyyah). It is said: at that moment, peace be upon him, reached such a level of confidence and lack of fear that he would put his hand into its mouth and take hold of its jaws.

Al-sirah is a form (fi'lah) from al-sayr, and it is used metaphorically for the manner and the form. Its being in the accusative may be explained in one of these ways: (1) by removing the preposition, i.e. ila siratiha (to its form); (2) that a'ada is transferred from 'adah, in the sense of 'ada ilayhi (returned to it); (3) as an adverb of place (zarfiyyah), i.e. We shall return it in its way; or (4) by supposing a verb for it and making it a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object, i.e. We shall return it as a staff as it was before, moving in its first course (sa'iratan sirataha al-ula), so that you benefit from it as you used to benefit before.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 22:

﴿And draw your hand to your side﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to do this after he had taken the serpent and it had returned to being a staff as it was before, meaning: put it under your upper arm, for the two wings (janah) of a human being are his two sides, just as the two wings (janah) of an army are its two flanks, a metaphor borrowed from the two wings of a bird. They were called two wings (janahayn) because the bird "yajnahuhuma", meaning it inclines them during flight. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿come forth﴾ is the answer to the imperative. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿white﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in it.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿without any harm﴾ is attached to an omitted element which is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in "white", meaning: existing without defect or ugliness. By it he meant leprosy (baras), just as he used "the evil" (al-saw'ah) as a euphemism for the private part (al-'awrah), because natures loathe it and recoil from it. It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) was of a brown complexion (adam), so he drew his hand out of his woollen garment (madra'ah) white, having a radiance like the radiance of the sun that dazzles the sight.

﴿another sign﴾ means: another miracle besides the staff. Its accusative is in the circumstantial position (al-hal), either from the pronoun in "come forth", as a substitute (badal) for the first circumstantial clause, or from the pronoun in "white". It has also been said that it is from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase, and it has also been said that it is in the accusative by an implied verb, such as "take" or "behind you" (khudh aw dunaka).

The phrase ﴿لِنُرِيَكَ مِن آياتِنا الكُبْرى﴾ is connected to an implied element that the noble structure of the discourse points to. It is as if it were said: "We did what We did, of commanding and manifesting, in order to show you by that some of Our greatest signs." This is on the basis that al-Kubra (the greatest) is an attribute of "ayatina" (Our signs). Or, "We show you by that, from among Our signs, those that are greatest," on the basis that al-Kubra is the second object of "linurayaka" (so that We may show you). And "min ayatina" (from among Our signs) is connected to a deleted element which is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of that object. In either case, the greatest sign (al-ayat al-kubra) refers to the staff and the hand together.

As for connecting it to what is indicated by a sign, i.e., "We demonstrated by them, so that We may show you..." etc., or to the words of the Exalted, "wadmum" (and draw in), or to "takhruj" (come out), or to what is estimated such as "khudh" (take) and "dunaka" (take hold of), as each of these has been said by a speaker, this leads to the sign of the staff being stripped of the description of greatness.

Then reflect. ﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾: this moves on to the real purpose after the preliminary introductions preceding it, and it is separated from the commands before it (in the form of a new sentence) to signal its importance. That is: go to him with the great signs you have seen, call him to worship Me, and warn him of My retribution. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, he has transgressed﴾ is a justification for the command, or for the obligation of the thing commanded: that is, he exceeded the limit in arrogance, haughtiness and tyranny, to the point that he dared to (p-12) the monstrous act, which is the claim to lordship.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 25:

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built upon a question that naturally occurs to the mind, as if it were said: "So what did he (peace be upon him) say when he was commanded with this grave matter and this arduous task?" It is answered: he said, seeking help from his Lord, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 26:

﴿And make my affair easy for me﴾. When he was commanded with what he was commanded of the momentous matter, he humbled himself before his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and displayed his incapacity by saying: ﴿And my breast tightens, and my tongue is not eloquent﴾. He asked the Exalted to expand his breast, widen his heart, and make him knowledgeable about the affairs of the Truth and the conditions of creation, forbearing and highly patient (ḥalīm ḥumūl), such that he would bear lightly whatever hardships and adversities might befall him, through beautiful patience and good steadfastness, receiving them with a spacious breast and a firm resolve. And [he asked] that, along with this, his affair, which is the most magnificent and greatest of matters and the most difficult and frightful of calamities, be made easy for him, through the facilitation of means and the removal of obstacles.

In the addition of the word "lī" (for me), while the speech is well-ordered without it, there is an emphasis on the request for expansion and facilitation, by first creating an ambiguity about what is expanded and what is made easy, and then explaining them afterward. In its placement before the two requests and its repetition, there is a display of greater concern for the matter of each of the two things sought, and an extra measure of earnestness in calling for their attainment for him and their being specific to him.

﴿And loosen the knot from my tongue.﴾ It is related that on his tongue, upon him be peace, there was a *ruttah* (a speech impediment) caused by a live coal that he put into his mouth in his childhood. The reason was that Pharaoh (Fir'awn) once carried him, and he seized his beard and began to pull at it because of the jewels that were in it. Pharaoh became angry and ordered that he be killed. Asiya said: "He is a child who cannot tell the difference between a coal and a ruby (*yaqut*)." So they brought the two of them before him, and he took the coal and put it in his mouth. It was said that his hand was burned, and Pharaoh strove to treat it but it did not heal. Then, when he (Moses) called on him, Pharaoh said: "To what Lord are you calling me?" He said: "To the One who healed my hand, which you have been unable to heal."

Scholars differ over whether the knot was removed completely. Whoever holds that it was removed relies on the words of God, Exalted: ﴿You have been granted your request﴾. Whoever does not hold that it was removed argues from the words of God, Exalted: ﴿He is more eloquent than I﴾, and His words: ﴿and he can hardly express himself clearly﴾. As for the first, the reply is that he did not ask for the knot of his tongue to be removed entirely, but only for a knot that prevents understanding. This is why he made it indefinite and described it with the words ﴿from my tongue﴾, meaning: a knot arising from the knots of my tongue.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 28:

He made His saying, ﴿that they may understand my speech﴾, the answer to the imperative (amr) and the purpose of the supplication (du'a'). So by the untying of the knot in general (fi al-jumlah), the granting of his request, upon him be prayers and peace, is realized. The truth is that what has been mentioned does not indicate that the knot remains in general. As for His saying, ﴿He is more eloquent than me﴾, it was said by him, upon him be prayers and peace, as a request for a solution (istid'a'an li-hall), as you will come to know. Moreover, his being more eloquent than him, upon both of them be prayers and peace, does not necessitate the knot's remaining at all; rather it necessitates its non-remaining, because eloquence (al-fasahah) entails the establishment of the basic eloquence even in the one who is less eloquent, and that is entirely incompatible with the knot (al-'uqdah) altogether. As for His saying, ﴿and he can hardly express himself clearly﴾, it is by way of exaggeration on the part of the accursed one in his arrogance and insolence, for otherwise it would indicate that the knot does not disappear at all. Its being indefinite (tankir) only indicates that it is little in itself, not little in relation to its being a part of much. The word "min" in His saying, ﴿from my tongue﴾, is connected to an omitted element which is its qualifier (sifah); it is not definitively so, rather the apparent view is that it is connected to the verb itself, for the thing untied, when it is attached to something and joined to it, then just as the untying is connected to it, that thing is also connected to it, in terms of its removal from it or the beginning of its occurrence from it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verses 29–30:

﴿And appoint for me a minister from my family﴾ ﴿Harun, my brother﴾. That is: one who gives me support (muwazir), who helps me bear the burdens of what You have charged me with. This is on the basis that its derivation is from the wizr (burden), which is weight; or [it means] a refuge (multaja') in whose opinion I seek protection, on the basis that it is from the wazar, which means refuge. It has also been said: its origin is azir, from al-azr (strength), on the pattern fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active participle), like al-'ashir (companion) and al-jalis (companion), its hamza being changed to a waw as in its change in muwazir. Its accusative case is because it is the second object of if'al (appoint), placed before the first object, which is His saying, exalted is He, "Harun", out of concern for the matter of the ministry (wizarah). And "li" (for me) is a complement to the act of appointing, or it is connected to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause (hal) from wazīran, since it is originally a qualifier of it. And "min ahli" (from my family) is either a qualifier of wazīran, or a complement of ij'al. It has been said: its two objects are "li" and "wazīran". "Harun" is an explicative apposition ('atf bayan) to "wazīran". "Min ahli", as has passed, is in both cases, and "akhi" (my brother) in both cases is a substitute (badal) for "Harun" or another explicative apposition. It has been said: they are [both] "wazīran" and "min ahli", and "li" is an explanation (tabyin), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and there is none comparable to Him, anyone﴾. It has been refuted on the ground that the condition for the two objects in the chapter of the abrogating particles (nawasikh) is the validity of forming a nominal sentence, and there is no way to make wazīran a subject (mubtada') about which what follows is predicated.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verses 31–32:

﴿Strengthen my back through him﴾ ﴿and make him a partner in my task﴾. Both are in the form of supplication (du'a'), meaning: make my strength firm through him, and make him a partner of mine in the matter of the message, so that we may cooperate in discharging it as it ought to be discharged. He separated the first from the preceding supplication (fasala) because of the complete connection between them (li-kamal al-ittisal bayna-huma), for "strengthening the back" is an expression for making him a vizier (wazir). As for "making him a partner in the matter," since it is among the requirements of the vizierate (min ahkam al-wizara), the conjunction (al-'atif) was placed between the two.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verses 31–32:

﴿Strengthen my back through him﴾ ﴿and make him a partner in my task﴾. Both are in the form of supplication (du'a'), meaning: make my strength firm through him, and make him a partner of mine in the matter of the message, so that we may cooperate in discharging it as it ought to be discharged. He separated the first from the preceding supplication (fasala) because of the complete connection between them (li-kamal al-ittisal bayna-huma), for "strengthening the back" is an expression for making him a vizier (wazir). As for "making him a partner in the matter," since it is among the requirements of the vizierate (min ahkam al-wizara), the conjunction (al-'atif) was placed between the two.

﴿That We may glorify You much﴾ ﴿and remember You much﴾ is a purpose (ghayah) for the last three supplications. If each of the two does, in those circumstances, tasbih (glorification) and dhikr (remembrance), then, since each one's joining with the other multiplies the other's effect, each one also increases the other's glorification and remembrance in itself, because their combined strength and mutual support reinforce it. What is meant by tasbih and dhikr is not what occurs between them inwardly in the heart or in private solitude, such that their state would not differ whether they are together or alone. Rather, it is what occurs between them in the course of conveying the message and calling the rebellious and obstinate tyrants to the truth. There is no doubt that their state differs between the two situations of being together and being alone, since each of them, through the support of the other, produces in the manifestation of the truth what would hardly be produced by one of them alone.

"Much" (kathiran) in both places is an adjective (na't) for a omitted verbal noun (masdar) or an omitted time (zaman), meaning: we exalt You above what does not befit You of attributes and acts, among which is what the tyrant Pharaoh claims, and what his rebellious faction accepts from him, namely the claim of partnership in divinity. And we describe You with what befits You of attributes of perfection and qualities of beauty and majesty, exalting You greatly (tanzihan kathiran), or [we exalt You for] a long time (zaman kathir), of which the time of Pharaoh's calling and the occasion of disputing with him is a part. As for what has been said, that the meaning is "that we may pray to You much and praise You and extol You," the context does not support it.

Verse: "Indeed You are ever Seeing of us" (or "You have always been, of us, All-Seeing").

Translation:

﴿Indeed You are ever Seeing of us﴾: that is, knowing of our circumstances, and that what You have called upon me for is of that which benefits us and aids us in accomplishing what You have charged me with, namely establishing the ceremonies of the message, and that Harun is an excellent helper (ridʾ) in carrying out what You have commanded. The bāʾ (in bi-nā, "of us") is connected to baṣīran (seeing), and it has been placed before it for the sake of observing the fawāṣil (verse-endings).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 36:

﴿He said: You have been given your request, O Moses.﴾ That is, you have been given your request. Su'l (request) here is in the form fu'l meaning maf'ul (that which is requested), like khubz (bread) and ukl (food) meaning makhbuz (that which is baked) and ma'kul (that which is eaten). And al-itha' (granting) is an expression for the connection of His, exalted is He, will to the occurrence of those requests and their absolute attainment by him, peace be upon him. His decree of them is definitive, so all of them are attained by him, peace be upon him, even though the actual occurrence of some of them is still awaited, such as the facilitation of the matter and the strengthening of his back. It is in this sense that it was said: ﴿We will strengthen your arm through your brother﴾.

His, exalted is He, saying ﴿O Moses﴾ is an honouring of him, peace be upon him, with the honour of direct address, following his honouring with the honour of having his supplication accepted.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 37:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We bestowed favor upon you another time﴾ is a resumptive statement (kalam mustanaf), driven to confirm what precedes it and to increase the soul of Musa, upon him be peace, in accepting it, by explaining that He, exalted is He, who bestowed upon him those perfect blessings without any prior supplication or request from him, then it is more fitting and more worthy that He bestow upon him the like of them when he is seeking it and calling upon Him. Its introduction with an oath (qasam) is for the utmost care given to that matter; that is: "By God, We have indeed bestowed favor."

﴿Another time﴾ means: at a time other than this time, not that this is postponed relative to that. For "ukhra" is the feminine of "akhar" in the sense of "ghayr" (other), and "al-marrah" (the time/occasion) originally is a noun for one passing; then it was applied to each single instance of the acts, whether transitive or intransitive; then it became common for each single individual of its instances, with numerous renewed individuals, so it became a standard term for that, until it was made a measure for what is similar in meaning among all other things. So it is said: this is the pattern of "marrah" (the form denoting one occurrence). Close to it are "karrah" (a return), "tarah" (a turn), and "dufʿah" (a push/instance). The intended meaning here is: the extended period during which there occurred what will be mentioned later of the great and numerous favors.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 38:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When We inspired in your mother that which is inspired﴾ is a temporal clause (zarf) governed by "We bestowed favour upon you" (manannā). By "inspiration" (al-iya') is meant either: inspiration through the tongue of a prophet at that time, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when I inspired the disciples...﴾ (the verse); or inspiration through the mediation of an angel, not in the manner of prophethood, as it was inspired to Mary; or inspiration in the sense of divine inspiration (ilham), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord inspired the bee﴾; or a vision (irada) in a dream. By "that which is inspired" is meant the command that would follow concerning casting him into the chest (tabut) and casting it into the sea, [namely] which of them first, to make it awe-inspiring and to magnify its importance; then it was explained so that it would be more reassuring to the soul. It has also been said that its meaning is: that which ought to be inspired and not neglected, because of its great importance and the extreme concern with it. It has also been said: that which cannot be known except through revelation. But this does not suit the last two meanings of inspiration, since there is no magnification of its importance in its being something that can only be known through divine inspiration (ilham), or through a vision (irada) in a dream.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 39:

(p-15) The "an" (أنَّ) in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Cast him into the chest﴾ (an iqdhifihi fi al-tabut) is either explanatory (mufassira), since revelation is of the category of speech, or it is a verbal particle (masdariyya) from which the preposition ba' has been dropped, meaning: "with [the command] that you cast him into it." The meaning of qadhf (casting) here is placing (al-wad'), whereas in His words ﴿then cast him into the river﴾ (faqdhifihi fi al-yamm) it means throwing (al-ilqa'). This distinction is what is meant by His words, exalted is He, ﴿And if you fear for him, then cast him into the river﴾, not casting without a chest.

﴿So let the river throw him onto the shore﴾ (falyulqihi al-yammu bil-sahil): since the river's casting him onto the shore was a matter that must occur, because the divine will is attached to it, the river is treated as if it were a discerning, obedient being that has been commanded to do this, and the answer is given in the form of a command. All the pronouns refer to Musa, peace be upon him. And although the thing cast into the river and thrown onto the shore is primarily the chest, since what is intended in essence is what is within it, the chest is made subordinate to him in this respect.

﴿An enemy to Me and an enemy to him will take him﴾ (ya'khudhhu 'aduwwun li wa 'aduwwun lahu) is an answer to the command to throw. The repetition of "enemy" is for emphasis and for explicitness about the matter, and to indicate that his enmity toward him, though certain, does not harm him or affect him, but rather leads to love. For the command to do something that is a cause of destruction is a form of casting him into the river and his falling into the hand of the enemy of God, exalted is He. And the word "enemy" indicates that there is a hidden kindness, concealed beneath an apparent subjugation. It is said that the first (the enemy to Me) is with respect to what actually happened, and the second (the enemy to him) with respect to what was expected. By "the shore" is not meant the bank itself, but what is opposite the middle, namely the part of the river adjacent to the shore, such that its water flows toward the Nile of Pharaoh. This is in accordance with what is narrated: she placed cotton in the chest, put him in it, then sealed it with pitch and cast it into the river. A small stream flowed from it to the garden of Pharaoh, and the water carried him to it and brought him to a pool in the garden. Pharaoh was sitting there with Asiya, daughter of Muzahim. He ordered it to be taken out and opened, and there was a boy, the most beautiful of people in face, and the enemy of God loved him with an intense love, hardly able to restrain himself from him. This is His words, exalted is He, ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ (wa alqaytu 'alayka mahabbatan minni). The word "min" (from) is connected to an omitted element, which is an adjective of "mahabbatan" that emphasizes what its indefiniteness conveys of grandeur by way of attribution: meaning, a great love originating from Me, which I have planted in hearts such that whoever sees you cannot help but be unable to bear being separated from you. For this reason the enemy of God and his household loved you. It is also said that it is connected to "alqaytu," meaning: I loved you, and whom God loves, hearts inevitably love.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿and that you may be reared under My eye﴾ (wa litusna'a 'ala 'ayni) are connected to "alqaytu," coordinated with a hidden purpose for it, meaning: so that he would be tender toward you, and that We might raise you with tenderness and compassion, under My watch and protection. Or it is connected to a hidden later element, which is an expression of what preceded it, namely the casting of love, and the clause is a new beginning, meaning: and that you be reared under My eye, I did that. It is read as "wa litusna'a" in the imperative form, with the lam vowelled with sukun and with kasra. It is also read with a fatha on the ta' and with the accusative, meaning: and that your action be under an eye of Mine, so that it would not be disobeyed concerning My command.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 40:**

﴿When your sister was walking﴾ is an adverbial complement (*zarf*) governed by ﴿and that you might be reared﴾ (*lituṣna'a*). The intended meaning is a time in which her walking took place, to the house of Pharaoh, and what followed from it of speech and her return to his mother, and her nursing him with kindness and tenderness. This is the fulfilment of His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿and that you might be reared under My eye﴾, since there is no compassion greater than the compassion of a mother and her care for him, in accordance with what He, exalted is He, requires of the guarding of it. It has also been said that it is a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿when We inspired﴾, on the basis that the intended meaning is a long period of time with widely separated extremities. This is the more suitable reading in light of what will follow, His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿So We delivered you from distress﴾ and so on, for all of that is among the divine favours, and none of them is connected to the aforementioned rearing. As for its being an adverbial complement of ﴿I cast﴾, as has been permitted, it may give the impression that the casting of love did not occur before that. There is no doubt that most of the effects of its casting appeared when the chest was opened.

﴿Then she says﴾, that is: to Pharaoh and Asiya, when she saw them seeking for him, peace be upon him, a wet-nurse whose breast he would accept, while he would accept no breast. The use of the present tense (*muḍāri'*) in the two verbs is to narrate a past situation vividly.

﴿Shall I direct you to one who will take charge of him?﴾, that is: who will take him into his own care and raise him. This would only happen by his accepting her breast. It is related that news spread in Egypt that the people of Pharaoh had taken a boy from the Nile who would not suckle the breast of any woman, and they were compelled to call upon the women. So his sister Maryam went out to learn his news, and she came to them disguised, and she said what she said and they said what they said. Then she brought his mother, and he accepted her breast. The *fa* in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿So We returned you to your mother﴾ is an explanatory *fa* (*fa' faṣīḥa*), indicating an omitted element before it, upon which what follows is coordinated. That is: they said, "Direct us to her," so she brought your mother, and We returned you to her.

﴿That her eye might be cooled﴾ by meeting you, ﴿and that she should not grieve﴾, that is: that grief should not come upon her by your separation after that. Otherwise, the removal of grief takes precedence over the joy expressed by "the cooling of the eye," since clearing away precedes adorning. It has been said: "and that you should not grieve," meaning you yourself should not grieve over the loss of her compassion.

﴿And you killed a soul﴾: it is the soul of the Copt whom the Israelite sought to help against him.

﴿So We delivered you from distress﴾, that is: the distress of killing him, out of fear of the punishment of Allah, exalted is He, by forgiveness, and from the retaliation of Pharaoh, by delivering you from it through emigration to Madyan.

﴿And We tried you with a trying﴾, that is: We tested you with a test; or "trials" from testing, on the basis that it is the plural of *fitan* or *fitnah* with the disregard of the *tā'* (feminine marker), like *ḥujūz* for *ḥujzah* and *budūr* for *badrah*. That is: We delivered you a second time. This is a summary of what he encountered in his journey of emigration from his homeland, the separation from familiar people, walking on foot, and the loss of provisions. It has been related that Sa'id ibn Jubayr asked Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, about it, and he said: "We delivered you from one ordeal after another. You were born in a year in which infants were being killed, and this is a trial, O son of Jubayr. Your mother cast you into the sea, and Pharaoh intended to kill you, and you killed a Copt, and you hired yourself out for ten years, and you lost the way, and your flock scattered on a dark night," and he would say at each one, "This is a trial, O son of Jubayr." However, what the noble composition requires is that his hiring himself out and what follows it not be counted among those trials, because the intended ones are what occurred before his arrival, peace be upon him, at Madyan, by the particle *fa'* in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿then you remained for years among the people of Madyan﴾. For there is no doubt that the aforementioned hiring and what follows it occurred after reaching them. By mentioning his, peace be upon him, staying among them, rather than his arrival at them, there is an indication of all the hardships and adversities he endured during those ten years, each of which is a trial, and what a trial!

Madyan is the town of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, eight stages from Egypt.

﴿Then you came﴾ to the place where fire was perceived and where the call and the cry occurred. The particle of delay (*thumma*) in the word indicates that his, peace be upon him, coming was after the great hardship, that being the loss of the way, the scattering of the flock on the dark winter night, and other things.

﴿At an appointed time﴾, that is: at the measure of Our decree, because I chose and appointed you for this at a time I had determined for it, so you came only at that appointed measure, neither ahead of it nor behind it. It has also been said: at a measure of time in which the prophets, peace be upon them, receive revelation, and that is at the age of forty years.

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿O Musa﴾ is an honouring of him, peace be upon him, and an alert that the narration has ended, which is the detailed account of the other occasion that occurred before the first narrated occasion.(p-17)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 41:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I have chosen you for Myself﴾ is a reminder of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I chose you﴾, and a preparation for his (peace be upon him) being sent to Pharaoh, supported by his brother, as He had requested after reminding him of the abundant favours that preceded, as a confirmation of his (peace be upon him) certainty that similar favours will come to him later. This is an illustration of the great honour that Almighty and Exalted God bestowed upon him by bringing him near to kingship, making him one of His special ones, and making him for Himself, and designating him for some of His grand affairs. The turning away from the plural of majesty in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We tried you﴾ and its two preceding counterparts is a preparation for the singular use of the word "self" (nafs), which suits the context, for it is more effective in realising the meaning of "making for oneself" (istina') and "selecting" (istikhlas). That is: I have chosen you for My messages and My speech.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 42:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Go, you and your brother﴾ — i.e., "And let your brother go as well, in accordance with what you were summoned to do." It is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to explain what is intended by the commissioning (al-istina').

﴿with My signs﴾ — i.e., with My miracles which I showed you, of the hand and the staff. For although they are two, in each of them there are various signs, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿In it are clear signs: the standing place of Ibrahim﴾. The transformation of the staff into a living creature is one sign; its being a great serpent whose magnitude cannot be measured is another sign; the swiftness of its movement together with the greatness of its body is another sign; and its being, along with that, subjected to him, peace be upon him, such that he would put his hand into its mouth and it would not harm him, is another sign; then its transformation back into a staff is another sign. Likewise the hand: its whiteness in itself is a sign, its radiance is a sign, and then its return to its original state is another sign. The bā' here is for accompaniment (li-l-musahabah), not for transitivity (li-l-ta'diyah), since the meaning is: their going to Pharaoh while clothed with the signs, holding fast to them in carrying out the rulings of the messengership and completing the matter of the call, not merely their taking them along and delivering them to him.

﴿and do not slacken﴾ — do not falter nor fall short. It has been read as "lā tanyā" with a kasra on the tā' for ease of pronunciation (li-l-ittiba').

﴿in My remembrance﴾ — i.e., by what befits Me of exalted attributes and beautiful deeds, at the time of conveying My message and calling to Me. It has been said that the meaning is: do not slacken in conveying My message, for remembrance (dhikr) applies to all acts of worship, and it is the most sublime and greatest of them. It has also been said: do not forget Me wherever you turn, and seek help and support through My remembrance. Know that no matter of affairs can be accomplished or made easy except through My remembrance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 43:

﴿Go, both of you, to Pharaoh﴾. He combined them in the imperative addressed to the present (second person dual), although Harun was absent, because the masculine plural/dual was given precedence (al-taghlib, the rule of giving precedence to one of two in grammatical address). The same applies to the prohibitive form. It is narrated that it was revealed to Harun, while he was in Egypt, that he should go out to meet Musa, peace be upon them both, and it was said: he heard of his approach and so went out to meet him.

﴿Indeed, he has transgressed﴾. This is a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the reason behind the command.

The fa' in His words ﴿So speak to him gently﴾ indicates that what follows is consequent upon his transgression, for gentle speech is among the things that break the fierce obstinacy of the stubborn and soften the disposition of tyrants. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Do not be harsh in your speech."
