It was also said: the gentle speech is like His words ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ and ﴿that I may guide you to your Lord﴾, for these are an invitation in the form of an offer and counsel. This is refuted by His words that come later, ﴿So go to him and say: Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord...﴾, the two verses.

It was also said that "gentle" refers to his kunya (teknonym), and he had three kunyas: Abu al-'Abbas, Abu al-Walid, and Abu Murrah. It was also said that it refers to the fact that he was granted a youth that does not age, and the pleasure of food and drink, and marriage and kingship, which would not end except by death.

It is also read as "لَيْنًا" (layyinan, with the vowel and the form of the word differing slightly in pronunciation from the standard reading "لَيِّنًا").

﴿Perhaps he will remember﴾ what you have conveyed to him of My remembrance, and will desire what you have made him desire.

﴿Or fear﴾ punishment. The clause (jumlah) is in the accusative position as a *hal* (circumstantial accusative) referring to the dual pronoun, meaning: speak to him gently, hoping that he will remember or fear. The word "أوْ" (aw, "or") here serves to preclude the absence of both, meaning: undertake the matter in the manner of one who hopes and aspires that his knowledge will bear fruit and his effort will not be in vain, and who strives with all his capacity and exerts his utmost. The benefit of sending the two of them to him, despite knowing his condition, is to establish the proof against him and cut off any excuse.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 45:

﴿They said: "Our Lord"﴾ The saying is attributed to both of them, although the one who actually spoke was Musa (peace be upon him), by way of taghlib (the dominance of one party within a dual reference), signifying that he is the principal in every saying and deed, and that Harun (peace be upon him) follows him in everything he does or leaves undone. It is also possible that Harun said that after they met, and so this was related together with the saying of Musa (peace be upon him) at the time the verse was revealed, just as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾. For this address has been related to us in the plural form, although each of those addressed was addressed only individually, since it is impossible for them to be gathered together in existence, so how could they be gathered together in address?

﴿Indeed we fear that he will hasten against us﴾ That is, that he will hasten to punish us, and not be patient until the completion of the call and the showing of the miracle, from faraṭa (to go ahead), when it means to precede. From it comes al-fārit (the forerunner), and a fāris fārit (a horse that outruns the horses). It has also been read as yufrita, from afrata, meaning he drove him to haste, i.e., we fear that some driver of arrogance, or fear for his kingdom, or something else, will drive him to hasten the punishment.

﴿Or that he will transgress﴾ That is, that he will increase in transgression until he says about your affair what is not fitting, due to the completeness of his audacity, harshness, and his freedom from good manners. The appearance of the word "an" (that), although the meaning is sound without it, serves to show full concern for the matter and to indicate the realization of fear from each of the two.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 46:

﴿Qāla﴾ (He said) is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf) built upon a question arising from the noble composition. Perhaps the attribution of the verb to the third-person pronoun is to indicate the shift of speech from one line to another, for what precedes it of verbs in the first-person form is a narration of Moses, peace be upon him, unlike what will come later in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We said, "Fear not; indeed you are the superior"﴾. For what precedes that too is narrated in the manner of narration to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is as if it were said: "What did their Lord say to them when they humbly entreated Him?" So it was said: "He said: ﴿Fear not﴾, that which you have imagined of the two matters."

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed I am with you both﴾ is a reason for the requirement of the prohibition, and an added consolation for them both. What is meant by "being with" is complete protection and support, as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿I hear and I see﴾ indicates, i.e., what passes between you two and him of speech and action; so I will do in every situation what befits it of averting harm and evil and bringing benefit and good. It is also permissible that nothing be supposed (as an object), in the sense that "I am your Guardian, Hearing and Seeing"; and the Guardian, the Helper, when he is such, then the support is complete and has reached its utmost limit.

﴿فَأْتِياهُ﴾ They were commanded to go to him and come before him, which is the meaning of arriving at him after being commanded to go to him. So there is no repetition. It is conjoined (*'atf*, grammatical coordination) with ﴿لا تَخافا﴾ (do not fear), with regard to its being the reason (*ta'lil*) given by what follows it. (p-19)

﴿فَقُولا إنّا رَسُولا رَبِّكَ﴾ They were commanded to say this to establish the truth from the very beginning, so that the tyrant (*al-Taghiyah*) would know their status and build his response upon it. Likewise is the mention of His lordship (*rububiyyah*, His being Lord) over him, exalted is He. The *fa'* in His statement ﴿فَأرْسِلْ مَعَنا بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ﴾ (so send with us the Children of Israel) is for putting what follows it in order after what precedes it, since their being the messengers of his Lord is among the things that necessitate sending the people with them. By "sending" is meant releasing them from captivity and coercion and bringing them out from under his oppressive hand, not obligating them to go with him to Syria with the two of them, as His statement ﴿وَلا تُعَذِّبْهُمْ﴾ (and do not torment them) indicates. That is, by leaving them in the torment they were in, for they were under the dominion of the Copts, who employed them in severe and crushing labor, such as digging, carrying stones, and other arduous tasks, and who would kill their male children in some years and not in others, and keep their women in service. The placing of the command to send between the statement of their message and the mention of coming with a sign that proves its validity is to show concern for it, together with what it contains of making the matter seem lighter to Pharaoh, since sending them with the two of them, without touching upon him and his people with various kinds of burdensome obligations, as is the usual nature of a mission, is not something that burdens him completely. Also, because mentioning the coming of the sign would be somewhat lengthy, as you see, postponing that would disrupt the harmony of the parts of the noble arrangement. As for what has been said, that this indicates that rescuing the believers from the disbelievers is more important than calling them to faith, then it is all [unsound].

﴿قَدْ جِئْناكَ بِآيَةٍ مِن رَبِّكَ﴾ (We have indeed come to you with a sign from your Lord) is an affirmation of what the preceding speech contained of the claim to messengerhood, and a reason for the necessity of sending them, since their coming with a sign from Him, exalted is He, establishes and confirms their messengerhood and makes obedience to their command obligatory. The explicit mention of the name "Lord" in the place of a pronoun, together with its being attached to the pronoun of address, is for emphasis on what was mentioned of the affirmation and the reasoning. The singular "sign" despite there being many is because the intent is to establish the claim by its proof, not to specify the multiplicity of the evidence. Likewise is His statement ﴿قَدْ جِئْتُكم بِبَيِّنَةٍ﴾ (I have indeed come to you with clear evidence), and His statement ﴿أوَلَوْ جِئْتُكَ بِشَيْءٍ مُبِينٍ﴾ (Even if I came to you with something clear?). As for His statement ﴿فَأْتِ بِآيَةٍ إنْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الصّادِقِينَ﴾ (Then bring a sign, if you are among the truthful), the apparent meaning is that by it is meant one sign among the signs.

﴿والسَّلامُ﴾ (And peace) is that which entails the safety of both abodes from Allah, exalted is He, and the angels and others among the Muslims.

﴿عَلى مَنِ اتَّبَعَ الهُدى﴾ (upon those who follow the guidance) by affirming the signs of Allah, exalted is He, which guide to the truth. In this is an encouragement to follow the two of them in the most gentle manner, which is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 48:

﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us﴾ from our Lord ﴿that the punishment﴾, both the worldly and the otherworldly, ﴿is for those who denied﴾, i.e., His signs, exalted is He, ﴿and turned away﴾, i.e., turned away from accepting them. In this there is a gentleness (talṭīf) in the warning, in that it did not explicitly state that the punishment would descend upon him, to an extent beyond which there is nothing more.

﴿Qāla﴾ (He said), that is, Pharaoh, after they had come to him and conveyed what they had been commanded. The mention of him has been omitted for brevity and to indicate that, as they had been commanded, they hastened to carry it out without hesitation, and that this matter is so evident that there is no need to state it explicitly.

﴿Fa-man Rabbukumā yā Mūsā﴾ (So who is the Lord of you both, O Moses?). He did not attribute the Lord to himself, not even by way of quoting what is said in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Innā rasūlā rabbika﴾ (Indeed we are two messengers of your Lord), and His words: ﴿Qad ji'nāka bi-āyatin min rabbika﴾ (We have certainly come to you with a sign from your Lord). This was due to the extent of his arrogance and the utmost of his tyranny. Rather, he attributed the Lord to the two of them, because the sender must necessarily be the lord of the messenger, or because the two of them had declared His lordship over all things, by saying: ﴿Innā rasūlu rabbi al-ʿālamīn﴾ (Indeed we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds), as occurred in (Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ). Limiting the mention here to His lordship over Pharaoh is sufficient for the purpose intended. The particle **الفاء** (fa) is for the sequencing of the question upon what preceded, namely that they are the two messengers of their Lord. That is: if you are the two messengers of your Lord, then tell me who is your Lord who sent you. The address is specifically directed to Moses, peace be upon him, while the address is directed to both of them, because he is the principal in the message, and Aaron is his minister.

As for what has been said, that this is because he (Pharaoh) knew that Moses, peace be upon him, had a speech impediment (**رتّة** ratta), so he wished to silence him and refute him by what he witnessed from him, peace be upon him, of excellent eloquence, which cut off that vain hope. As for his words: ﴿Wa-lā yakādu yubīn﴾ (and he can hardly express himself clearly), it is due to his extreme wickedness and corruption, as has already been mentioned. (p-20)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 50:

﴿Said﴾ i.e., Musa, peace be upon him, answering him.

﴿Our Lord﴾ is either a subject (mubtada'), and His saying, ﴿Who gave everything its creation﴾, is its predicate (khabar). Or it is a predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject, and the relative clause is its attribute (sifa). In either case, by the first-person pronoun they did not mean only themselves, as the accursed one intended, but all created beings, to establish the truth and refute him. This is made clear by what is within the relative clause, i.e., He is our Lord who gave everything among things its creation, meaning its form and shape suited to what has been assigned to it of distinctive features and benefits; or He gave His creatures everything they need and from which they benefit. The fronting of the second object is for emphasis on it. Or He gave every animal its counterpart in creation and form, since He paired the stallion with the mare, the camel with the she-camel, and man with woman, and He did not pair anything of these with something other than its own kind. It is also read as "khalaqahu" in the past tense, with the clause then being an attribute of the genitive-governing noun or of the noun governed by it; the second object is omitted either for restricting the verb to the first object, i.e., every thing God the Exalted created, He did not deprive of His bounty and favour, or for brevity, its being intended and indicated by the context, i.e., He gave everything God the Exalted created what it needs.

﴿Then guided﴾ i.e., to the way of benefiting from and making use of what He has given. He taught it how to reach its survival and perfection, either by choice, as in animals, or by nature, as in inanimate things and the natural vegetative and animal powers. Since creation, which is the composition of parts and the shaping of bodies, precedes guidance, which is the implanting in those bodies of the motive and perceptive powers, the particle of delay (thumma) was placed between them. Peace be upon him, he presented his answer in a delightful manner and fitting style, showing that He, the Exalted, is knowing and powerful by essence, the creator of all things, bestowing upon them everything fitting for them by way of grace. He also implied that His sending Musa to the tyrant is among His guidances after He guided him to the truth through the created guidances, in that He composed in him the intellect and the other senses and the outward and inward faculties.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 51:

﴿He said: "Then what is the state of the earlier generations?"﴾ When the accursed one (al-La'in, i.e., Iblis/the adversary) saw that the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, had arranged in the thread of argument a clear proof of splendid design, he feared that he would make manifest to the people the reality of his (i.e., the Prophet's) statements and the falsity of the fabrications of his own self, manifest and clear. So he wished to divert him, upon him be blessings and peace, from his ways toward matters that concern him, namely narratives having no connection to the Message, and to occupy him from what he was engaged in, hoping that some kind of heedlessness would appear in him, so that he might thereby ascend to claim before his people some kind of knowledge. So he said: "What is the condition of the past generations and the bygone nations, and what detailed events befell them?" The Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, answered that knowledge of their conditions in detail is something that has no connection with the office of Prophethood, and that its knowledge is only with Allah, Mighty and Majestic. As for what has been said, that he asked him about the state of those generations that passed away, and about the wretchedness of those among them who were wretched and the felicity of those who were felicitous, then this is rejected (lit. "it is refused by this").

(p-21) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: "Its knowledge is with my Lord"﴾. Its meaning is that it is among the unseen matters that none knows except Allah, may He be exalted. I am only a servant, and I know of them only what He has taught me of the matters connected with that with which I have been sent. Had the matter asked about been what was mentioned of wretchedness and felicity, he would have been answered with an explanation that whoever followed the guidance among them has been safe, and whoever turned away has been punished, as expressed by His saying, may He be exalted: "And peace be upon..." (the two verses).

﴿In a Book﴾, that is: recorded in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) in its details. It is permissible that this be a figurative expression for its firmness (tamkkun) and for its being established in the knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by what the Knowing One entrusted to be preserved and recorded by the scribes (al-kataba), as His saying, may He be exalted, alludes to: ﴿My Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾, that is: He does not make a mistake at the outset, and His knowledge does not vanish with time, but is established forever, for both of these are impossible for Him, glorified is He. The first (negation) serves to show that its being recorded in the Tablet is not due to any need on His part for it in knowing it, whether at the outset or afterward. The manifestation of "my Lord" in the place where a pronoun would be expected serves to delight in mentioning Him, to add firmness (taqrir), and to indicate the reason for the ruling, since lordship (rububiyyah) necessarily requires not erring and not forgetting.

And he, peace be upon him, answered the question with a wondrous and original answer, for he unveiled the veil from the reality of the Truth, although he did not depart from what he was engaged in, namely explaining His exalted attributes. Then he moved on to Him, saying, by way of relating what God, Mighty and Majestic, said, in anticipation of the later iltifat (shift from third-person speech to first-person speech): ﴿Who made the earth for you a cradle﴾. This is on the basis that the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is either in the nominative, as a laudatory construction (madh), or in the accusative by the same logic, or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: He made it for you like a cradle, in which you settle it, or possessing a cradle (mahd), which is a verbal noun used as a name for the object. It is also read as "mihadan" (a bed), which is a name for that which is spread out, like a carpet, or the plural of mahd, meaning: He made every place in it a cradle for each one of you.

﴿And threaded for you therein roads﴾, that is, He provided you with paths, and placed them between the mountains, valleys and deserts, which you traverse from one region to another, so that you may fulfil your needs from them and benefit from their advantages and amenities.

﴿And sent down from the sky water﴾, which is rain, ﴿and We brought forth by it﴾, that is, by that water. This is a conjunction with "sent down" and falls under the relating of speech (hikaya). The shift to the first-person plural was made to draw attention to the manifest evidence in it of perfect power and wisdom, and to indicate that it cannot come about except from one who is capable, obeyed, and great in station, to whose command diverse things submit and to whose will they yield, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen that God sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth by it fruits of diverse colours?﴾ and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth, and sent down for you water from the sky, and We caused to grow by it gardens of delightful beauty﴾. Except that what precedes the shift there is the direct speech of God, exalted is He, whereas here it is a relating of His speech. He made His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and We brought forth by it﴾ the reported speech, although what precedes it is the speech of Musa, peace be upon him, which is contrary to the apparent meaning; moreover, that would then nullify the iltifat because the speaker is not the same.

﴿Pairs﴾, that is, kinds. They were so named because they are paired, and some of them are joined to others.

﴿Of vegetation﴾ is an explanation or a qualifier of "pairs", meaning: existing from vegetation. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿diverse﴾, that is, scattered, the plural of shatit. It is permissible for it to be a qualifier of "vegetation", since it is originally a verbal noun in which the singular and plural are the same. The meaning is that they are diverse, differing in taste, smell, shape and benefit: some of them are fit for people in the various ways of benefit, and some for beasts. For indeed, part of the completion of His blessing, exalted is He, is that since the provision of His servants is obtained through the labour of livestock, He made their fodder from what exceeds their needs, and it is not fitting for it to be food for them. (p-22)

"And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Eat and graze your livestock﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in ﴿So We brought forth﴾, on the understanding of an implied saying (ʿalā irādat al-qawl). That is: We brought forth from it various kinds of plants, saying: Eat and graze your livestock, i.e., (We are) preparing them for your benefit, both directly and indirectly, giving permission for that."

"﴿Indeed in that﴾ is a demonstrative pointing to what was mentioned of His affairs and acts, exalted is He, and the distance implied in it is to signal the lofty rank of His station and the remoteness of His position in perfection. The indefiniteness in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿signs﴾ is for magnification, both in quantity and in quality; that is: there are many, sublime signs, clear in their indication of the affairs of God, Exalted is He, in His essence, attributes and acts, and of the soundness of the prophethood of Moses and Aaron, upon them be peace."

"﴿For people of understanding (ūlī al-nuhā)﴾: the plural of nuhya, by which the intellect is named because it restrains (nahy) from following falsehood and committing abominations, just as it is named ʿaql (intellect/restraint) and ḥijr (restraint) because it binds and restrains from that. That is: for those possessed of intellects that forbid vanities, among which is what the tyrant claims and what his rebellious faction accepts from him. The specification of these as signs for them, although they are signs for all who have knowledge, is on the basis that they are the ones who benefit from them."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 55:

﴿From it We created you﴾ That is: within your father Adam, upon him be prayers and peace, from it. For every single individual of mankind has a share in his creation (peace be upon him), since his unique natural constitution (fitra) was not confined to himself (peace be upon him), but was rather a prototype (unmudhaj) containing within it, in a summary manner (intiwa' ijmali), the natural constitution of all the other members of the species, with the effects of that constitution necessarily flowing over all of them. Thus his creation (peace be upon him) from it was a creation of all of them from it. It has been said: the meaning is: We created your bodies from the semen (nutfa) produced from foods, which were produced from the earth through intermediaries. It has also been said: the angel charged with the womb takes some of the soil of the place where the newborn will be buried and scatters it upon the semen, and so he creates from the dust and the semen.

﴿And into it We shall return you﴾ by death and the dispersal of the parts. The choice of the word "fi" (in) rather than "ila" (to) indicates a lengthy settling within it.

﴿And from it We shall bring you forth once more﴾ by reassembling your scattered parts, which have been mixed with the dust, into their former form, and returning the spirits to them. That this bringing forth is "once more" is because your creation from the earth is a bringing forth of you from it, though not in the manner of the second occasion. The word "tara" (occasion) originally denotes a single turn (tawr), namely a movement, and then it was applied to each single act among repeated acts, as was explained regarding "marra" (time).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 56:

﴿And indeed We showed him﴾ is a summary narration of what took place between Musa (peace be upon him) and Fir'awn, following the narration of the mighty favours that Musa (peace be upon him) had mentioned, favours which called Fir'awn to accept the truth and submit to it. Introducing it with an oath serves to demonstrate the utmost concern with its content. Attributing the showing to the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah), looking at the reality and not to Musa, is in view of the reality and not merely the apparent; it serves to magnify the matter of the signs and to exalt their status, and to show the completeness of their manifestness to the eye and Fir'awn's persistence in obstinacy and hostility. That is: by Allah, We indeed made Fir'awn see them, or made him know them.

﴿Our signs﴾: when he said to Musa (peace be upon him): ﴿If you have come with a sign, then produce it, if you are of the truthful.﴾ ﴿So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent.﴾ ﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the beholders.﴾ The use of the plural form, although they are two, is in view of the wondrous matters within them, each of which is a clear sign for a people who reason, as has been explained in the commentary on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs.﴾ Certain other matters appeared before Fir'awn, each of which was a great calamity. It is narrated that when he (peace be upon him) threw it, it turned into a serpent, a huge one, opening its mouth wide, between whose jaws there were eighty cubits; it placed its lower jaw on the ground and its upper jaw on the wall of the palace, and it turned toward Fir'awn, who fled, defecated, and the people fled in a crowd, so that twenty-five thousand of his people died. Fir'awn cried out: "O Musa, I adjure you by the One who sent you, take it!" So he took it, and it returned to a staff. It is also narrated that it turned into a snake that rose in the sky the distance of a mile, then descended approaching Fir'awn, and began to say: "O Musa, command me with whatever you wish," while Fir'awn said: "I adjure you ..." etc. And when he drew his hand out of his collar, behold, it was white with a luminous whiteness beyond the limits of customary things, whose radiance overcame the radiance of the sun, and onlookers gathered around it in amazement at his matter. Thus within each of the two signs there are many signs, but since they were not mentioned explicitly, they were emphasised by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿all of them﴾, as if it were said: We showed him Our signs with all their consequences and details, intending to make clear that no excuse whatsoever remained for him in this. There is no justification for counting the remaining nine signs among them, since they manifested at the hand of (peace be upon him) only after the sorcerers had been overcome gradually over roughly twenty years, as has passed in the commentary on Surat al-A'raf. There is no doubt that the matter of the sorcerers is still awaited afterward, and it is even further removed to count among them what was made for their destruction and not for guiding them to faith, such as the splitting of the sea, and what appeared after its destruction of the manifest signs for the Children of Isra'il, such as the lifting of the mountain and the rock, whether by the rock that fled with its garment or the rock from which the springs gushed forth. Likewise, it is not proper to count among them the manifest signs at the hands of the prophets (peace be upon them all), on the basis that his (peace be upon him) narrating them to Fir'awn is tantamount to displaying them before him, and his showing them to him is by the impossibility of lying upon him (peace be upon him); for his narrating them to Fir'awn is something whose mention has not occurred here. Moreover, what will come of interpreting what he displayed (peace be upon him) as sorcery and as a challenge to counter-contest with the like clearly rejects this and declares decisively that what is meant by them is what we have mentioned; were it not so, it would be permissible to make what he (peace be upon him) detailed of the acts of Allah, Exalted is He, which indicate His exclusive lordship and its rulings, among the signs.

﴿But he denied﴾: Musa (peace be upon him) denied, without hesitation or delay, despite what he witnessed in his hand of the evident proofs of his truthfulness, out of obstinacy and hostility. ﴿And refused﴾ faith and obedience, because of his haughtiness and arrogance. It has been said: he denied all the signs and refused to accept any of them, or refused to accept the truth.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 57:

And His saying, ﴿He said: "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land with your sorcery, O Moses?"﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the manner of his denial and refusal. The interrogative particle (hamza) is for denying what has occurred and deeming it abominable, and claiming that it is an impossible matter. The "coming" (majī') is either in its literal sense, or in the sense of turning toward a matter and undertaking it, meaning: "Have you come to us from your place in which you were after you had been absent from us, or have you turned toward us to drive us out of Egypt by what you have displayed of sorcery? For that is something that does not proceed from a rational person, since it belongs to the category of attempting the impossible." He said this in order to incite his people to extreme hatred of Moses, peace be upon him, by making clear that his aim, peace be upon him, was not merely the rescue of the Children of Israel from their hands, but the expulsion of the Copts from their homeland and the complete seizure of their wealth and properties, so that no one would turn to following him, and so that they would exert themselves in resistance and contention. The miraculous sign that he, peace be upon him, displayed, the evident miracle, was called "sorcery" in order to embolden them to confront it, then he claimed that he would oppose it (p-24) with the like of what he, peace be upon him, had brought.

Then he said: ﴿So we will surely bring you magic like it.﴾ The fa' (فَ) indicates that what follows is a consequence of what precedes it. The lam (لَ) is the answer to an implied oath, as if it were said: "If that is the case, then by God, we will surely bring you magic like your magic."

﴿So set between us and you an appointment.﴾ That is, a promise, as indicated by its description in His words, exalted is He, ﴿which we will not break﴾, since the promise is what fits here, not the place or the time. That is, we will not break that promise.

﴿Neither we nor you.﴾ The accursed one delegated the matter of the appointment to Moses, peace be upon him, in order to avoid being attributed with weakness of heart, narrowness of ground, or a display of boldness, and in order to show that he was able to prepare the means of opposition and arrange the instruments of contest, however long or short the time. Likewise, placing his pronoun before the pronoun of Moses, peace be upon him, and inserting the negative particle between them, signals his haste in not breaking the appointment, and that his not breaking it does not necessitate Moses's breaking it, peace be upon him. For this reason the negation is emphasized by repeating its particle. As for the accusative (naṣb, نَصْب) of ﴿a place equidistant﴾ (مَكانًا سُوًى), it is governed by a verb indicated by the verbal noun (maṣdar), not by the verbal noun itself, since the latter is a modified noun; or it is in apposition (badal, بَدَل) to "appointment," on the assumption of an implied place as a genitive complement.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 59:

Then the correspondence of the answer in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your appointment is the day of adornment﴾ is in terms of meaning, for the day of adornment (yawm al-zinah) indicates a place well known for people gathering in it on that day; or by supposing "a place like the place of your appointment" to be "the place of the day of adornment," as it is in the first case; or "your promise is the promise of the day of adornment." It has been read as "yawma" in the accusative, and this is clear that what is meant by it is the verbal noun (masdar). The meaning of "suwan" (a level, equal place) is a midpoint whose distance is equal for us and for you. In terms of qualification it is like their saying "qawm 'Adiyy" (the people of 'Adiyy) as an anomaly (shudhudh). It has also been read with a kasra on the sin. It is said: the day of adornment is the day of 'Ashura', or the day of Nawruz, or a festival day that they had every year. The Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, specified it by definition only to show the perfection of his strength and that he was confident of his matter and unconcerned with them, because that day was the time when the full extent of their power would appear, and so that the manifestation of the truth and the vanishing of falsehood would take place on a famous day before the eyes of the witnesses, and that would spread among every present and absent person.

﴿And that the people be gathered at forenoon﴾ is conjoined to "a day" or "the day of adornment." It has been read in the active voice with the ta' (addressing Pharaoh), and with the ya' (third person), on the basis that the pronoun refers to him according to the custom of kings, or refers to the day.

﴿So Pharaoh turned away﴾, i.e., he withdrew from the assembly. ﴿Then he gathered his stratagem﴾, i.e., what is used as a stratagem against (the Prophet Musa), namely the sorcerers and their implements. ﴿Then he came﴾, i.e., to the appointed place, bringing with him what he had gathered of his stratagem. In the word "thumma" (then), which denotes delay, there is an indication that he did not hasten to it, but came to it after hesitation and dithering.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 61:

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Moses said to them﴾, etc. By way of a resumptive statement (istinaf) built upon a question, it implies that what was awaited from his state, upon him be peace, at that time, and what needed a question and an explanation, was nothing but what proceeded from him, upon him be peace, of speech. As for his coming first, it is a established matter that needs no explicit mention. It is as if it were said: "What did Moses, upon him be peace, do when Pharaoh came with what he had gathered of the sorcerers?" So it was said: He said to them, by way of advice: ﴿Woe to you! Do not fabricate against Allah (p-25) a lie﴾, by calling His signs, which will appear at his hands, sorcery, as Pharaoh did. ﴿Lest He destroy you﴾, that is, He will uproot you because of it, ﴿with a punishment﴾ that is terrible, whose extent cannot be measured. It was also read "yasḥitakum" from the triliteral (root), according to the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, while al-ISHAT (ishat, the causative form) is the dialect of the Banu Tamim and Najd.

﴿And he has indeed failed who fabricates﴾, that is, against Allah, whoever he may be and in whatever manner it may be, so that the forbidden fabrication enters into it by primary inclusion; or, "and Pharaoh, the fabricator, has indeed failed," so do not be like him in failure. The sentence is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ) confirming the content of what precedes it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 62:

﴿So they disputed⁠ ﴾ — that is, the magicians, when they heard his words, peace be upon him, as if that enraged them. ﴿So they disputed their affair⁠ ﴾ — the matter that was intended from them, namely overcoming him, peace be upon him, and they consulted and deliberated ﴿among themselves⁠ ﴾ about the manner of opposition, and they tugged at the edges of speech concerning that. ﴿And they conspired in secret⁠ ﴾ — that is, away from Moses, peace be upon him, lest he become aware of it and repel them.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 63:**

Their secret talk was what is expressed in the words of God Most High: ﴿They said﴾, that is, by way of private consultation (*tanajī*) and in secret, ﴿Indeed, these two are certainly magicians﴾, and so on. This is an explanation of it, a result of their disputing, and the summary of what their opinions settled upon after debate and consultation. ﴿Inna﴾ is the lightened form of *anna* and has been stripped of its grammatical effect, and the *lām* is the *lām al-fāriqa* (the distinguishing *lām*). It has also been read with the *nūn* of ﴿hādhāni﴾ doubled. It has been said that ﴿inna﴾ is a negative particle, and the *lām* means *illā* (except), so the meaning is: ﴿These two are none but magicians﴾. It has been read as ﴿inna﴾ with the doubled *nūn*, with ﴿hādhāni﴾ as its subject, according to the dialect of Bilḥārith ibn Ka'b, for they treat the dual as indeclinable, marking it by a fixed form. It has been said that its subject is the omitted dummy pronoun (*ḍamīr al-sha'n*), and ﴿wa-hādhāni la-sāḥirāni﴾ is its predicate. It has been said that ﴿inna﴾ here means ﴿naʿam﴾ (yes), and what follows it is a sentence consisting of a subject and a predicate. Against both of these views is that the *lām* does not enter the predicate of a nominal sentence. It has been said that the original was ﴿innahu hādhāni lahumā sāḥirāni﴾, and the pronoun was omitted; against this is that what is emphasised by the *lām* does not admit omission. It has also been read as ﴿in hādhayni la-sāḥirāni﴾, and this reading is clear.

﴿They both want to drive you out of your land﴾, that is, the land of Egypt, by seizing control of it, ﴿by their magic﴾ which they displayed earlier, ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾, that is, with your creed, which is the best and most excellent of creeds, by making their own creed prevail and raising their religion. By this they mean what the people of Pharaoh were upon, not the way of magic, for they did not regard it as a religion. It has also been said that they meant the people of your way, namely the Children of Israel, in reference to the words of Moses (peace be upon him): ﴿Send with us the Children of Israel﴾, and they were men of knowledge among themselves. Against this is that driving them out of their land would only come about through seizing control of it in the sense of establishing dominion and disposing of it, so how could the transfer of the Children of Israel to the Levant (*al-Shām*) then be imagined? And to take the driving out as the expulsion of the Children of Israel from it while the people of Pharaoh remain as they are is something by which the revelation must be held free, all the more so since this statement from them was meant to incite the pursuit of vigorous opposition and the earnest pursuit of enmity. Therefore the warning and admonition must be with the most hateful and most grievous things for them, and there is no doubt that removing the Children of Israel from their sons and taking them to the Levant while they are safe in their homes involves little that is to be feared. It has also been said that ﴿al-ṭarīqa﴾ is a name for the notables and nobles of a people, since they are exemplars for others. It is not hidden that singling them out for the removal is something in which there is no distinction.

(p-26) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So marshal your scheme﴾ is an explicit statement of the goal after laying out the premises. The fa' is fasihah (the fa' that signals an implied condition), meaning: since the matter is as mentioned, namely that these two are sorcerers, and they intend to drive you out and eliminate you as has been described, then resolve upon your scheme and make it something agreed upon, such that none of you deviates from it, and shoot together from one bow. It was also read as fajma'u from al-jam' (gathering), and His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿then he gathered his scheme﴾ supports it. That is: gather the implements of your magic and arrange them as they should be arranged.

﴿Then come forward in a row﴾, that is, lined up in rows. They were commanded to do so because it is more awe-inspiring in the hearts of the onlookers and more effective in drawing dread from the spectators. It is said there were seventy thousand, each with a rope and a staff, and they came forward together as one. It is also said they were seventy-two sorcerers: two from the Copts and the rest from the Children of Israel. And it is said: nine hundred from the Persians, three hundred from the Romans, and three hundred from Alexandria. It is said: fifteen thousand, and it is said: some thirty-odd thousand, and God knows best. Perhaps the place of appointment was a wide area: Musa, upon him be peace, addressed them with what he mentioned in one region of it, and they disputed their affair in another region of it, then they were commanded to come to its middle in the manner mentioned. The saf (row) has been interpreted as the musalla (place of prayer), since people gather there for the festivals and the prayers; its soundness lies in its being a proper name for a specific place within the appointed area. But taking it to mean one of the many places of prayer after the appointed place had been determined has no justification whatsoever.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he has succeeded today who prevails﴾ is an interjected concluding remark from their side, reinforcing what preceded it of the two matters. That is: whoever prevails has won the goal. By "the goal" they mean what Pharaoh had promised them of reward and nearness, as expressed in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near."﴾ And by "whoever prevails" they mean prevailing over all of themselves, in the manner of their saying: ﴿By the might of Pharaoh, we are indeed the victors.﴾ Or it means whoever among them is overcome, urging them to exert their utmost effort in the contest. This is what suits the harmony of the parts of the noble composition. It has been said: their secret conference was when they heard the words of Musa, upon him be peace: "This is not the speech of a sorcerer." It has also been said: it was their saying, "If Musa overcomes us, we will follow him." And it has been said that it was their saying: "If he is a sorcerer, we will surely overcome him, and if he is from heaven, then he has a command." Their whispering would then have been from Pharaoh and his chiefs, and their saying ﴿"Indeed these two are surely sorcerers"﴾ ... etc. is to be understood as meaning that they disagreed among themselves according to the views mentioned, then returned from that after dispute and debate, and their opinions settled upon that, and they refused anything but opposition for the sake of contesting. As for making the pronoun in "they said" refer to Pharaoh and his chiefs, on the basis that they said that to the sorcerers to turn them away from disagreement, and commanded them to unite and resolve, and to display steadfastness by coming forward in ranks, this undermines the eloquence of the noble composition, as sound taste attests.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 65:

﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), answering a question that arises from the narrative of what passed between the sorcerers in their discussion. It is as if it were said: "What did they do after they had said among themselves what they said?" So it is said: they said, ﴿O Musa﴾. As for not dwelling on their gathering and their coming in ranks (iṣṭiffāf), this is to indicate that their affair was evident and that they were independent of explanation.

﴿Either you throw﴾, i.e., what we throw first, with the object omitted because it is evident; or you perform the throwing first, with the verb treated as intransitive (munazzal manzilat al-lazim).

﴿Or we will be the first to throw﴾, i.e., what he throws, or the first to perform the throwing. They gave him the choice, peace and blessings be upon him, in these terms, out of consideration for courtesy, given what they saw from him, peace and blessings be upon him, of the signs of goodness and the steadiness of judgment, and to display firmness, by showing that their state would not differ whether they went first or second. "An" (that) together with what follows it is either in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb, or in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: choose your throwing first, or our throwing; or the matter is either your throwing or our throwing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 66:

﴿He said﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), as previously noted, arising from the narration of the sorcerers' offering him the choice, as if it were asked: "What did he (peace be upon him) say then?" And it is answered: he said: ﴿Rather, you throw﴾ first yourselves, in contrast to the courtesy of their manners with a better courtesy, since they had stated outright the matter of their throwing first, and to show indifference to their sorcery, and to assist what they had given the impression of, the inclination to begin, and that they might bring forth what they have, exhaust their utmost effort, and expend the best of their power; then Allah, mighty and majestic, manifests His authority, so He hurls the truth upon the falsehood and it crushes it, since He knew that what would appear by his hand would swallow up what they were crafting of the schemes of sorcery.

﴿So behold, their ropes and their staffs, it was imagined to him, because of their sorcery, that they were moving﴾ The fa' (fa') is an eloquent particle (fa' fasihah), indicating the speed of their casting, as in His saying, Exalted is He: "So We said: Strike the sea with your staff, and it split" (Q 26:63), meaning: so they threw. ﴿So behold, their ropes﴾ "Idha" (idha) here is for sudden surprise and affirmation, and it is also a temporal adverb (zarfiyyah) that requires a complement governing it and a clause to which it is added; but it is specifically restricted to the case where its complement is the verb of surprise, and the clause is inceptive (ibtida'iyyah). The meaning: so they threw, and Musa (peace be upon him) was suddenly confronted at the moment it was imagined to him that the ropes and staffs were moving, because of their sorcery. That was because they had smeared them with mercury, and when the sun struck them they vibrated and shook, so it was imagined to him that they were moving. It has been read as "tukhayyalu" (with ta') by attributing it to the pronoun of the ropes and staffs, with "annaha tas'a" substituted for it as a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal). It has been read as "yukhayyalu" by attributing it to Him, exalted is He. It has been read as "takhayyala" by eliding one of the two ta's from "tatakhayyalu".

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 67:

﴿So Musa conceived within himself a sense of fear﴾. That is, he harboured in himself some fear of being taken by surprise by it, in keeping with the human nature that is disposed to recoil from snakes and to guard against their usual harm, such as their bite and the like. It has also been said: [he feared] that doubt might creep into the people so that they would not follow him. But this is not the case, as you will come to know. And the placement of the subject after the verb is for the sake of observing the fawasil (the verse-endings).

[Qur'an 20:68] "We said: Do not fear" — that is, do not entertain what you imagined. "Indeed, you are the superior one" — this is a justification for what the prohibition requires, namely ceasing to fear, and an affirmation of his dominance in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, as indicated by the resumptive construction (al-isti'naf), the particle of emphasis (harf al-tahqiq), the repetition of the pronoun, the definiteness of the predicate (ta'rif al-khabar), the word "superior" (al-'ulluw), which indicates evident dominance, and the superlative form (sigha al-tafdil).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 69:

﴿And throw down what is in your right hand﴾, that is, your staff, as occurred in (Surah al-A'raf). The indefiniteness (ibham) is either chosen to magnify its matter and exalt its status, and to signal that it is not of the kind of ordinary staffs (ʿiṣiyy) that bring about the customary effects, but is beyond the limits of all individuals of the kind, its essence undefined, and it brings about strange effects. Not observing this subtlety when the matter is related in another place does not necessitate not observing it when this narrated event occurred. Taking the indefiniteness as belittling, meaning "do not care about the multitude of their ropes and staffs, and throw down the little stick that is in your hand, for by the power of Allah the Exalted it will swallow them, despite its oneness and their multitude, its smallness and their greatness," is contradicted by the appearance of its condition in what passed twice. Moreover, that meaning would only be fitting if the staff had done what it did while in its original form, whereas in fact it had already done what it did.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿it will swallow what they have made﴾, with the jussive (bi-l-jazm) as an answer to the imperative, from laqifa, meaning: when he swallows something and seizes it swiftly. The feminine form is because "ma" refers to the staff, i.e., it will swallow what they have made of ropes and staffs, which were imagined to you as moving and agile. The expression "what they have made" is for belittling, and to indicate deception and falsification. It has been read as "talaqqafu" with the qaf doubled and one of the two taʾs dropped from "tatalaqqafu". It has also been read in the nominative (raf'), as a circumstantial clause (hal) or as a resumptive sentence (isti'naf). The imperative clause is coordinated with the prohibition and completes what is within its scope, to give the reason for its requirement by explaining the manner of his, peace and blessings be upon him, victory over them and his superiority. For the swallowing of his staff of their falsehoods, among which he had sensed what he had sensed of fear, is something that uproots their substance entirely. This, as you see, is clear that his fear, peace and blessings be upon him, was not of the doubt that troubles people and their not following him, peace and blessings be upon him; otherwise it would have been explained by what removes it, namely the promise, by which their belief and following of him, peace and blessings be upon him, would be required.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, what they have made﴾ etc., is a reason for His saying, ﴿it will swallow what they have made﴾. The "ma" is either a relative pronoun or a qualifying noun, i.e., indeed what they have made, or indeed a thing they have made, ﴿is the plot of a magician﴾, with the nominative as predicate, as if to say the plot of the category of magician. Its indefiniteness is a means to indefinite the thing it is annexed to, for belittling. It has been read in the accusative, as the object of "they have made", with "ma" being a restrictive particle (kafffa). It has been read "kaydu sihrin" with the annexation being explanatory, as in "ilmu fiqhin," or in the sense of "one possessing magic," or as naming the magician "magic" for emphasis.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the magician does not prosper﴾, i.e., this category, ﴿wherever he comes﴾, i.e., wherever he is, and wherever he comes from, is part of the completion of the reason, and it does not address the matter of the staff, nor that it is a divine miracle, although that would strengthen the reason, as an indication of the manifestation of its affair.

The fa' in His words, ﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate﴾, as explained earlier, is *fasiha* (the fa' that signals an unstated antecedent). It indicates two omitted elements that the noble text clearly implies, and which need not be stated explicitly, since it is not possible that Musa, peace be upon him, hesitated to obey the command or that the promised casting would fail to occur. The meaning is: he, peace be upon him, cast it, and what happened of the casting happened. Then the magicians were thrown down prostrate when they became certain that this was not a matter of magic, but rather one of the signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is narrated that their leader said: "We used to overcome people, and our ropes would remain intact for us. So if this were magic, where are the ropes we cast?" He inferred from the change in the states of bodies the existence of the Creator, the Powerful, the All-Knowing, and from this manifestation at the hand of Musa, peace be upon him, the truth of his prophethood. Therefore, what they had witnessed threw them onto their faces, and they repented, believed, and performed the utmost form of submission. It has been said: they did not raise their heads until they saw Paradise and Hell, and the reward and the punishment. And it is reported from Ikrimah: when they fell prostrate, Allah, Exalted, showed them in their prostration their dwellings in Paradise. This does not contradict their saying: ﴿Indeed we have believed in our Lord that He may forgive us our sins﴾ etc., because those dwellings being theirs is in consideration of the utterance of this statement by them.

﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*), as has passed more than once. ﴿We have believed in the Lord of Harun and Musa﴾: the mention of Musa is delayed when recounting their words for the sake of observing the rhyme (*fawasil*). It has also been permitted that the order of their speech be like this as well, either because of the old age of Harun, peace be upon him, or for the sake of thoroughly guarding against the false suspicion on the part of Pharaoh and his people, since Pharaoh was the lord of Musa, peace be upon him. For had they mentioned Musa, peace be upon him, first, the accursed one and his people might have suspected from the very beginning (p-29) that their intended meaning was Pharaoh.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 71:

﴿Qāla﴾ i.e., Pharaoh said to the magicians, ﴿"Have you believed in him"﴾ i.e., in Mūsā (upon him be peace), and the lām here is included to imply the meaning of following (ittibā'). It is also read as an interrogative of reproach (istifhām tawbīkhī).

﴿"Before I gave you permission"﴾ i.e., without my having given you permission to believe in him, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"Even if the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord are exhausted"﴾. It does not mean that his permission to them in this matter came afterwards or was expected.

﴿"Indeed, he"﴾ meaning Mūsā (upon him be peace), ﴿"is your chief"﴾ i.e., in your craft, the one who knows it best, and your teacher, ﴿"who taught you magic."﴾ So you colluded in what you did; or [it means] he taught you one thing and not another, and that is why he overcame you. This is a testimony that the accursed one fabricated and cast upon his people, showing them that the matter of faith depends on his permission. Since their belief was without his permission, it had no standing, and since they were among his pupils (upon him be peace), no weight is to be given to what he [Mūsā] displayed, just as no weight is to be given to what they displayed. This was because of the fear that had overtaken him, lest people follow the magicians in believing in God Exalted. Then he turned to them with an emphatic threat, saying: ﴿"So I will surely cut off"﴾ i.e., by God, I will surely cut off ﴿"your hands and your feet on opposite sides"﴾, i.e., the right hand and the left foot. The "min" here is ibtidā'iyya (indicating starting point), as if the cutting begins from the opposition of one limb to another, for the one who starts from the side of the one presented also starts from the side of the one afflicting. It and its genitive are in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyya), i.e., "I will surely cut them off, being opposed." Specifying that state is to announce the matter's certainty and its inevitable execution by specifying its known manner in the domain of statecraft, not because it is more horrible than other manners.

﴿"And I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees"﴾ i.e., upon them. The choice of the word "fī" (in) indicates keeping them on them for a long time, likening their continuance on them to the settling of the contained within the container that encloses it. They said: he was the first to crucify. The form taf'īl in both verbs indicates intensification, and both have also been read with the lighter form.

﴿"And you will surely know which of us"﴾ he means himself and Mūsā (upon him be peace), due to his saying: ﴿"You believed in him before I gave you permission"﴾. The lām with "īmān" in the Book of God is for other than Him, Exalted; and this is either for the purpose of belittling Mūsā (upon him be peace) and mocking him, since he had no part in the punishment, or to show that their faith was not from witnessing the miracle and beholding the proof, but was from fear of Mūsā (upon him be peace), since they saw the swallowing of their ropes and staffs by his staff, so they feared for themselves as well. It was also said: he means by it the Lord of Mūsā, in whom they believed by their saying: ﴿"We have believed in the Lord of Hārūn and Mūsā"﴾.

﴿"Harsher in punishment and more lasting"﴾ i.e., more enduring.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 72:

﴿They said﴾, being unconcerned with his threat: ﴿We will never prefer you﴾, meaning, we will never choose you in faith and following, ﴿over the clear proofs that have come to us﴾ from Allah through Musa, peace be upon him, ﴿from the clear proofs﴾, meaning the manifest miracles. For what appeared through the staff in the hand of Musa, peace be upon him, comprised many of his miracles, as its verification was discussed previously, since they knew its grandeur and its subtleties.

﴿And Him who created us﴾, that is, who created us and all other creatures. It is coordinated with ﴿what has come to us﴾. Its delay is because what is contained within it is a rational, theoretical sign, whereas what they witnessed is a manifest sensory sign. The mention of Him by the title of His being our Creator, exalted is He, is for the sake of indicating the cause of the ruling, for His being our Creator and Fir'awn being among His created beings necessitates that they not prefer him over (p-30) Him, glorified and exalted is He. This is a reply from them to the rebuke of Fir'awn in his saying: ﴿Have you believed in him before I give you permission?﴾ It has also been said that it is an oath whose answer is omitted, the mentioned part indicating it, meaning: "By the One who created us, we will never prefer you…" etc. There is no basis for the mentioned clause to be its answer according to those who permit placing the answer first as well, because an oath is not answered by "lan" except by an anomaly. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So decree what you will decree﴾ is a reply to his threat in his saying: "I will surely cut off…" etc., meaning: do what you are going to do, or judge what you are going to judge. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You only decree concerning this worldly life﴾, together with what follows it, is a justification for the indifference derived from what preceded of the command to decree, meaning: you only do what you desire, or judge by what you see, in this worldly life alone, and we have no desire for its pleasures nor fear of its punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 73:

﴿Indeed, we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins﴾ which we committed therein of disbelief and disobedience, and that He not hold us accountable for them in the Hereafter, not so that He would let us enjoy that transient life until we are affected by what You have threatened us with of cutting off and crucifixion. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the sorcery to which you compelled us﴾ is a conjunction with "our sins," meaning: and that He forgive us the sorcery which we learned in opposing Moses, peace be upon him, through Your compulsion and Your gathering of us from the distant cities. They singled it out for mention, although it is included among their sins, to show the extreme of their aversion to it and their desire for its forgiveness. And mentioning the compulsion serves as a notification that it is among the things that must be singled out for seeking forgiveness, even though it proceeded from them under compulsion, and there is in it a kind of apology to attract forgiveness. It has also been said: they meant compulsion to learn sorcery, for it is narrated that their chiefs were seventy-two, two of them from the Copts, and the rest from the Children of Israel, and Pharaoh had compelled them to learn sorcery. And it has been said: he compelled them to the opposition, for it is narrated that they said to Pharaoh: "Show us Moses asleep," so he did, and they found his staff guarding him, so they said: "This is not sorcery, for when the sorcerer sleeps his sorcery is nullified," but he refused except that they should oppose him. What contradicts this is their eagerness for the opposition with desire and zeal, as their saying indicates: ﴿Shall we indeed have a reward if we are the victors?﴾ and their saying: ﴿By the might of Pharaoh, indeed we are the victors﴾.

﴿And Allah is better﴾ meaning: in His own essence, and it looks to their saying: ﴿and He who originated us﴾.

﴿and more enduring﴾ meaning: in recompense, whether reward or punishment; He is better in reward and more enduring in punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 74:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he﴾ up to the end of the two conditional clauses, is a justification from their side, for His being "better and more enduring" is a recompense and a confirmation of it, and a refutation of what Pharaoh claimed. Their introduction with the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n) serves to alert to the grandeur of their content, because the basis for placing the pronoun in its position is the claim of its being well known, which is sufficient without mentioning it, together with the added emphasis it carries. For the pronoun is not understood from it at first except as an ambiguous matter of great importance, so the mind remains expectant of what follows it, and thus when it arrives it takes firm hold with exceptional firmness. It is as if it were said: The matter of great importance is this, namely His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal﴾, by dying in disbelief and sins, ﴿for him is Hell; he will neither die therein﴾, so that his punishment would end, and this is a confirmation that His punishment is more enduring, ﴿nor will he live﴾ a life by which he benefits.

﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer﴾ in Him, the Exalted, and in what came from Him of miracles, among which is what we have witnessed, ﴿has done righteous deeds﴾. *Salihah* (righteous): like *hasanah*, it functions as a noun, and for this reason it is generally not mentioned together with the noun it qualifies. It is every deed that is upright according to the evidence of reason ('aql) and transmitted evidence (naql).

﴿Then those﴾ refers back to "whoever" (man), and the plural is used in view of its meaning, just as the singular in the two preceding verbs is used in view of its wording. The sense of distance in "those" indicates the elevated rank and lofty standing of these people. That is, "those" are the believers who do righteous deeds. ﴿For them﴾, because of their faith and their righteous deeds, ﴿are the lofty ranks﴾, i.e., the exalted stations. There is nothing in this verse that indicates that bare faith without righteous deeds is disregarded in entailing reward, because what is attached to faith combined with righteous deeds is attaining the lofty ranks, not reward in an absolute sense. And is the dispute about anything other than this?

The Qur'anic phrases are rendered in plain English within the ﴿ ﴾ markers.

﴿Gardens of perpetual residence﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, in grammar an apposition replacing the preceding noun) of "the high ranks," or else a *bayan* (explanatory apposition). It has already been explained that *Adn* (Eden) is a proper noun denoting either the sense of permanent residence or the land of Paradise. The words ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ are a *hal* (circumstantial clause) describing the gardens. The words ﴿wherein they abide forever﴾ are a *hal* describing the pronoun in "for them." The governing element of this *hal* is either the sense of settledness (*al-istiqrar*) or the demonstrative meaning.

﴿That﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the success they have been granted through the high ranks just mentioned. The sense of distance in the demonstrative is for the purpose of exalting the matter, as stated earlier.

﴿is the recompense of whoever purifies himself﴾, meaning whoever cleanses himself of the filth of disbelief and sins through the faith and righteous deeds already mentioned. This confirms that His reward, may He be exalted, is more lasting. The mention of the state of the criminal is placed first in order to hasten to explain the greater severity and perpetuity of his punishment, in refutation of what Pharaoh claimed in his words: ﴿Which of us has the harsher and more lasting punishment?﴾

It has also been said that these three verses are the beginning of a new statement from God, mighty and majestic. They said: the Qur'an does not state that Pharaoh did to those believers what he threatened them with, and it is not established in the reports.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 77:

﴿And We certainly revealed to Musa﴾ This is a summary narrative of what the affair of Fir'awn and his people came to. Between this and that, the mention of what befell them of the detailed, manifest signs at the hand of Musa, upon him be peace, after he overcame the magicians, is omitted, about some twenty years, as detailed in (Surat al-A'raf). Its introduction with an oath serves to show the utmost care for its content. The "an" in His words, exalted is He, ﴿that travel by night with My servants﴾ is either explanatory (mufassira), because revelation (wahy) carries the meaning of saying, or it is a verbal (masdariyya) "an" from which the preposition has been omitted. The expression of them by the title of being His servants, exalted and majestic is He, serves to show mercy and concern for their affair, and to draw attention to the extreme ugliness of Fir'awn's conduct toward them, in that he enslaved them while they were the servants of Him, exalted and majestic, and did to them every kind of injustice that he did. That is: and by Allah, We certainly revealed to him, upon him be peace, that travel by night with My servants whom We sent you to rescue from the dominion of Fir'awn, that is: travel with them out of Egypt by night.

﴿So strike for them﴾ That is: make, or take for them, ﴿a dry path in the sea﴾ That is: dry, (the word being) a verbal noun (masdar) described by the agent for emphasis. It was also read as "yabsan," which is either a lightened form of it, or an adjective like "sa'b," or a plural of "yabis" like "sahb," used of the singular for emphasis, or because it is multiple according to the number of the tribes (asbat).

﴿Fear not being overtaken﴾ This is a circumstantial clause (hal) of the one commanded, that is: safe from the enemy overtaking you; or it is another attribute of "tariqan," with a omitted returning pronoun. It was also read as "la takhaf" as an answer to the imperative.

﴿And do not fear﴾ This is a conjunction with "la takhafu," falling under its ruling, that is: and do not fear drowning. On the reading with the jussive, it is a new sentence, that is: and you do not fear, or it is conjoined to it, and the alif is for pausal lengthening, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿and you assume about Allah assumptions﴾. The placing before of the negation of the fear mentioned is for hastening to remove the great fear they had, when they said: ﴿Indeed, we are surely overtaken﴾.

**(Surah 20, verse 78)**

﴿So Pharaoh followed them with his hosts﴾. That is: he followed them, with his armies, until they caught up with them. It is said: *atba'tuhum* means "I followed them," and this is used when they had gone ahead of you and you caught up with them. This is supported by the reading "*fa-atba'ahum*" (فَأتْبَعَهُمْ) in the *iftiʿāl* (the eighth verbal form, *ifti'āl*, which here carries the sense of following after), which is a recitation attributed to some readers. It was also said: the meaning is that Pharaoh himself followed them, so the second object was omitted. It was also said: the *bāʾ* in *bi-junūdihi* is redundant, and the meaning is: Pharaoh followed them with his armies, that is, he drove them behind them. Whichever of these is the case, the *fāʾ* (in *fa-atba'ahum*) is *faṣīḥah* (the "eloquent *fāʾ*," a *fāʾ* that signals an omitted clause understood from the context), indicating an implied element whose mention was dropped, relying on how plainly it is evident and to announce the complete eagerness of Moses, peace be upon him, to comply with the command. The implied sense is: so he did what he was commanded, namely, to travel by night with them and to strike the path and take it, and Pharaoh followed them with his hosts, by land and by sea. It is narrated that Moses, peace be upon him, set out with them at the beginning of the night, and they numbered six hundred and seventy thousand. Pharaoh was informed of this and followed them with his armies, and his vanguard was seven hundred thousand. He traced their trail and caught up with them, to the point that the two hosts saw each other. At that moment, peace be upon him, he struck the sea with his staff, and it split into twelve parts, each part like a great mountain. Moses, peace be upon him, crossed with those who were with him of the tribes safely, and Pharaoh followed them with his hosts.

﴿Then the sea covered them with what covered them﴾. That is: it overcame them, and what overwhelmed them of the terrible matter, whose extent cannot be measured and whose reality cannot be grasped. It was also said: "what covered them" means that the story of it was heard, but this is not the point, for the core of the awe and grandeur lies in its exceeding the limits of understanding and description, not in the hearing of its story. It is also read: "*fa-ghashshāhum min al-yammi mā ghashshāhum*" (فَغَشّاهُمْ مِنَ اليَمِّ ما غَشّاهُمْ), meaning: covered them what covered them. The agent is God, Mighty and Exalted, or "what" (the thing that covered them). It was said the agent is Pharaoh, because he was the one who plunged them into destruction.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 79:

And the explicit mention in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray﴾, rules this out. That is, he took them on a course that brought them to loss and ruin in both religion and worldly life together, since they died in disbelief and were struck with a terrible worldly punishment that was joined to the everlasting punishment of the Hereafter.

And His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and he did not guide﴾, that is, he never once guided them to a path leading to any of the aims, religious or worldly. It is a confirmation and an emphasis of his misguiding them, since one who misleads may sometimes guide those he misleads to some of their aims. There is also a kind of mockery of him in His words: ﴿And I guide you only to the path of right conduct﴾. For denying guidance from a person implies that he is one from whom guidance could in some sense be expected, and this can only be imagined regarding him in the manner of mockery. Taking "misleading" and "guiding" to refer to what pertains to religion from among them is ruled out by the context, which describes his driving his soldiers to the path of worldly destruction, and by making them an expression for misguidance into the sea and for deliverance from it, which a sound intellect cannot accept.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 80:

﴿O Children of Israel﴾ is a narration of what Allah the Exalted addressed to them after He drowned Pharaoh and his people and delivered them from them. However, it was not immediately after that, but after He had bestowed upon them the various kinds of religious and worldly blessings that He bestowed. It has been said that it is the initiation of an address to those who were among them in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), in the sense that He, the Exalted, bestowed favour upon them by what He did to their forefathers directly and to them indirectly. This is refuted by His words that follow: ﴿And what hastened you away from your people...﴾ (20:83), since it is impossible to read it as a fresh address. Therefore, the correct reading is that it is a narration, with the implied verb "We said" (qulna) coordinated with "We revealed" (awhayna), meaning: "And We said: O Children of Israel, ﴿We have delivered you from your enemy﴾ Pharaoh and his people, since they used to plot against you ruin, ﴿and they subjected you to a dreadful torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women﴾." It is also read as "najjaynakum" and "najjaytukum."

﴿And We made a covenant with you at the right side of the Mount﴾. The word "jānib" (side) is in the accusative (naṣb), as it is an attributive adjective of the noun it modifies, and it is also read in the genitive (jarr) by attraction to the adjacent word. The meaning is: We made a appointment with you through your prophet to come to its right side, viewed from the perspective of one traveling from Egypt to Syria. That is, the appointment was for Moses, upon him be peace, to come for private conversation with Allah and for the descent of the Torah upon him. The appointment is attributed to them even though it was for Moses, upon him be peace, in consideration of its connection to them, the spread of its benefit to them, and in order to give the station of bestowing favour its due, as in His words: ﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you﴾ (7:11), where creation and fashioning are attributed to the addressees, although the one directly created and fashioned was Adam, upon him be peace. It is also read as "wa'adtukum" and "wa'adnakum."

﴿And We sent down upon you the manna and the quails﴾. That is, the tarnjabin (a sweet exudation) and the quails. The manna would descend upon them while they were in the wilderness of wandering (al-tih), like snow, from dawn until sunrise, a ṣā' for each person. The south wind would bring quails to them, and a man would slaughter from them what sufficed him, as has passed several times.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 81:

﴿Eat﴾ is a resumptive clause (jumla musta'nafa), brought in to explain the permissibility of what was mentioned to them and to complete the blessing upon them. ﴿of the good things We have provided for you﴾, i.e., of their delights (ladha'idh), or of their lawful things (halalat). It is also read "razaqtukum" (I provided for you). In beginning with the blessing of deliverance, then with the religious blessing, then with the worldly blessing, there is of fine arrangement (husn al-nazm) and subtle ordering (lutf al-tartib) what is not hidden.

﴿And do not transgress therein﴾, i.e., concerning what We have provided for you, by failing to give thanks for it and by exceeding what has been set as limits for you concerning it, such as extravagance (israf), arrogance (bataran), and withholding from one who deserves it.

﴿Lest My anger descend upon you﴾ is an answer to the prohibition, i.e., then My punishment will be binding upon you and due for you, from halla al-dayn, when its payment became due (wajabaada'uhu).

﴿And whoever has My anger descend upon him, then he has fallen﴾, i.e., he has been ruined and perished. It was said: he fell into the Abyss (al-Hawiya). It is also read "fayahulla" with a damma on the ha', from halla yahullu, when it descended (nazala).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 82:

﴿And indeed I am Most Forgiving toward those who repent﴾ from shirk (associating partners with God) and from the sins, among which is transgression in what has been mentioned, ﴿and believe﴾ in what belief in it is obligatory, ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾; that is, they do righteous deeds that are upright according to the Sharia and reason. In this is an encouragement for whoever has fallen into transgression in what has been mentioned, and an exhortation to repentance and faith.

And the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then remained guided﴾, that is, remained steadfast upon guidance (istiqamah), indicate that whoever does not persist in it is not exempt from forgiveness. And "thumma" (then) here denotes a gradation in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 83:

﴿And what has hastened you away from your people, O Musa?﴾ This is a narration of what took place between Allah, exalted is He, and Musa, upon him be peace, of speech at the beginning of his arrival at the appointed time, in accordance with the promise mentioned earlier. That is: We said to him, "What has hastened you, alone, away from your people?" As you see, this is a question about the reason for his going ahead of the chiefs (nuqaba', the representatives of the tribes). It is directed at denouncing his separating himself from them, because that, outwardly, carries signs of their being neglected and of not being given any regard, although he had been commanded to take them along and bring them with him. It is not a denunciation of hastiness itself, which proceeded from him, upon him be peace, since it would be a deficiency incompatible with the resolve befitting the people of firm resolve (uli al-'azm).

Therefore, peace and blessings be upon him, responded to Him by denying that he had gone ahead alone, which would contradict keeping company and being together, when [the Qur'an says] ﴿"They are right behind me"﴾, meaning: they are with me. I had only outpaced them by a small distance, which I thought would neither break the togetherness nor detract from the companionship, for such a gap is not regarded at all among fellow travellers.

After he, peace be upon him, mentioned that his going ahead was not for a reprehensible matter, he mentioned that it was for a matter that is pleasing, when he said: ﴿"And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased"﴾ with me, by my hurrying to carry out Your command and my care in fulfilling Your covenant. The addition of "my Lord" (rabbi) is for greater supplication and entreaty, desiring acceptance of the excuse.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 85:

﴿Said [He]﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) answering a question arising from the narration of his (ﷺ) excuse, namely Moses, peace be upon him. This is the reason it comes in the third-person form, and it is not a shift (iltifat) from the first person to the third, because the implied speaker in the two previous places was in the first-person form, as if it were said by the listeners. So what did his Lord say to him at that time? It is said: He said: ﴿Indeed, We have tested your people after you﴾, i.e., We tried them with the worship of the calf after your departure from among them.
