They are the ones whom he left behind with Aaron, peace be upon him, and they were six hundred thousand; of them, only twelve thousand were saved from worshipping the calf.

The fa' (so) indicates the sequence of the report of the trial mentioned upon the report to Moses, peace be upon him, of his people's haste. However, it is not because the report of it is a cause necessitating the report of the other, but because of the connection between them that justifies moving from one to the other, in that the basis of the mentioned trial is the haste of the people. It is related that they remained, in accordance with what Moses, peace be upon him, had enjoined upon them, for twenty nights after his departure, and they counted them together with their days as forty, and said: "We have completed the term," and there was no sign or trace of Moses, peace be upon him.

﴿And the Samiri misled them﴾, since he was the one who planned the trial. He said to them: "Moses, peace be upon him, has only broken his promise to you because of the ornaments of the people that you have with you, and they are forbidden to you." So what happened with the calf happened. God, exalted is He, informed him of the occurrence of this trial at his (Moses') arrival, either by way of its being realized in His knowledge and will, or by way of expressing what is expected by what has occurred, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out﴾ and its like, or because the Samiri had resolved to bring about the trial at Moses' departure and had undertaken to arrange its foundations and prepare its beginnings, so the trial was regarded as occurring at the time of the report of it. It was read: "And the Samiri misled them" in the comparative form, meaning: he was the most misguided of them, because he was both astray and a misleader.

Al-Samiri (al-Sāmirī) is ascribed to a tribe of the Children of Israel called al-Sāmirah. It is said that he was a non-Arab (ʿilj) from Kirman, and it is said that he was from the people of Bajarma. His name was Musa ibn Zafar, and he was a hypocrite who had outwardly professed Islam, and he was from a people who worshipped cows.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 86:**

﴿So Musa returned to his people﴾ at his customary return, that is, after he had completed the forty nights and received the Torah, not immediately after being informed of the trial. The causal sense of what precedes the *fa'* (the particle of consequence) applies to what follows it only through the qualifier of return derived from the words of the Exalted: (p-35) ﴿angry and grieved﴾. It is not the return itself as such that is the cause, even though it is in fact included. The return occurring after the completion of the forty days is a fixed and well-known matter, so the mind does not go to the idea that it happened at the time of the report about the trial. This is like when you say: "I accompanied the pilgrims and prayed for their safety, and they returned safe," where no one doubts that the intended meaning is their customary return, not their return right after the prayer. The causal link of the prayer is through the attribute of safety, not through the return itself. *Al-asif* means one who is extremely angry; it is also said to mean one who is grieved.

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*) answering an implied question arising from the account of his return. It is as if it were said: "What did he do to them?" So it is said: he said, ﴿O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise﴾, namely that He would give you the Torah, containing light and guidance. The *hamza* (interrogative particle) here is for denying the non-occurrence of the promise and affirming its occurrence in the most emphatic and forceful manner. That is: He promised you in a way that leaves you no path to denying it.

As for the *fa'* in the words of the Exalted, ﴿Has the time seemed long to you?﴾, *al-'ahd* means the time. It is a conjunction linking to an implied clause, and the *hamza* is for denying only what is conjoined, namely the lengthening of time. That is: "I promised you that, then the period of its fulfilment grew long, so you erred by reason of it."

﴿Or did you intend that there should descend﴾, that is, become binding, ﴿upon you wrath﴾, a severe wrath whose extent cannot be measured, ﴿from your Lord﴾, that is, from the Owner of your affairs absolutely.

﴿So you broke your appointment with me﴾, that is, your promise to me to remain steadfast in what I commanded you until I return from the appointed place. The verbal noun is here attributed to its object, intending to increase the reproach of their condition. Their breaking of the promise made between them and him, peace be upon him, is more grievous when it is attributed to him, peace be upon him, than when it is attributed to them. The *fa'* indicates that what follows it is the consequence of each of the two parts of the disjunction, taken as alternatives. It is as if it were said: "Did you forget the promise through the lengthening of time, so that you broke it by mistake? Or did you intend for wrath to descend upon you, so that you broke it deliberately?" As for taking the appointment as attributed to its agent and understanding its breaking as the sense of finding a breach in it, namely: "you found a breach in my promise to you of returning after forty days," this is not supported by the context (*sibaq*) or the wider context (*siyaq*) at all.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 87:

﴿They said: "We did not break our promise to you of our own power﴾. That is, our promise to you was firm, in accordance with what you commanded us. Its being expressed as "our promise" (mawidatuna) rather than "our breaking" is through the idafa of the verbal noun to its agent, as has passed just before.

﴿"By our own power"﴾. That is, by our power over our affairs. They mean: had we been left to our own affairs, and had the Samiri not embellished for us what he embellished, along with the assistance of some circumstances, we would not have broken it. It is also read as "bi-malkina" with kasra and with damma on the mim, and all are dialects for the verbal noun of malaktu al-shay' (I possessed the thing).

﴿"But we were made to carry burdens of the people's ornaments"﴾. This is an exception to what preceded, and an excuse for what they did by explaining the source of the error. It is also read as "humelna" (without the doubling), meaning: we carried loads of the jewelry of the Copts, which we had borrowed from them when we were resolved to leave Egypt under the pretext of a wedding. It was said that they had borrowed it for a festival they held, and then did not return it to them when they departed, out of fear that they would learn of their plan. It was also said: it is what the sea cast onto the shore after their drowning, and they took it. Perhaps their calling them "burdens" is because they were liabilities and sins, since spoils were not lawful at that time.

﴿"So we threw it"﴾. That is, into the fire, hoping for deliverance from its sin. ﴿"So likewise"﴾, that is, in the same manner as that throwing, ﴿"threw the Samiri"﴾, that is, what he had of it. He had shown them that he too would cast what he had of the jewelry, and so they said what they said according to their supposition. What he cast was only the dust he had taken from the footprint of the Messenger, as will come. It is narrated that he said to them: "Moses delayed from you only because of the burdens you carry. So the opinion is that we dig a pit, kindle a fire in it, and cast into it everything we have." So they did this.

﴿So he brought forth﴾, that is, the Samiri, ﴿for them﴾, for those who said it, ﴿a calf﴾, made from those melted ornaments. Placing it [the object] after the prepositional phrase, even though it is an explicit object (mafʿul sarih), is for the reason already mentioned many times: to give prominence to what is fronted and to create anticipation for what follows. At the same time, placing it first would involve a kind of lengthiness that would disrupt the correspondence of the parts of the noble arrangement (al-nazm al-karim). As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿a body﴾, that is, a corpse having blood and flesh, or a body of gold with no spirit, it is a substitute (badal) for it. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that had a lowing﴾, that is, the sound of a calf, is a qualifier (naʿt) for it.

﴿Then they said﴾, that is, the Samiri and whoever was seduced by him when he first saw it: ﴿This is your god and the god of Moses, but he [Moses] forgot﴾, that is, he [Moses] neglected Him and went off to seek Him at Mount Tur. This is a narration of the result of the Samiri's seduction, in both deed and speech, from Him, exalted is He, intentionally, in order to increase its establishment, and then to direct the denunciation toward it, not from the side of those who spoke. Otherwise, it would have been said: "Make for us [a god]." The interpretation that their shift to the third-person pronoun is to show that the bringing forth and the statement mentioned belong to all of them, not only to the worshippers, is contrary to the apparent meaning, and moreover it undermines their excuse. For the fact that some of them opposed the Samiri and were not seduced by his enticement, while the bringing forth and the address were directed at them as well, is something that makes their opposition to him easier to bear for those making the excuse. Therefore, their being seduced after that is a greater crime and more shameful. As for what has been said, that those making the excuse are those who did not worship the calf, and that attributing the breaking of the promise to themselves, while they were innocent of it, is of the kind of saying "the sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so," even though only one of them was the killer, as if they said: "No breaking of the promise was found among us by a matter we controlled; rather, doubt took hold in the hearts of the worshippers when the Samiri did what he did, brought forth for them what he brought forth, and said what he said, so we could not turn them away from that, and we did not leave them for fear that the seduction would increase." This is refuted by the coherence (siyaq) and the context (sibaq) of the noble arrangement, which requires its corruption.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 89:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not see?﴾ and so on, is a rebuke and a reproach from Him, exalted is He, concerning the state of both the astray and those who lead others astray, and a declaration of their foolishness in what they have undertaken of the reprehensible matter whose falsehood and impossibility are not unclear to anyone, namely taking it as a god. The fa' (fa) here is for conjunction (al-'atf) upon an implied clause required by the context, meaning: "Do they not reflect, so that they would know?" ﴿Does it not return to them a word?﴾ That is, it does not return to them any speech, nor does it answer them with any reply, so how could they imagine that it is a god? It has also been read as "yarji'a" with the accusative case. They said: in that case the seeing is visual (basariyyah), for the nasiba (the particle an) does not occur after verbs of certainty (af'al al-yaqin), meaning: "Do they not look so that they would perceive the absence of its returning to them any word of any kind?" Linking the perceiving to what has been mentioned, although it is a non-existent matter, serves to draw attention to its complete clarity, which calls for greater condemnation of them and belittling of their minds.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it has no power to harm them or benefit them﴾ is a conjunction upon "does not return," included together with it within the scope of seeing, meaning: "Do they not see that it has no power to ward off harm from them or bring them benefit, or that it has no power to harm them if they do not worship it, or to benefit them if they do worship it?"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 90:

﴿And indeed Aaron had already said to them before﴾ This is an oath-clause (jumla qasamiyya) emphasizing what precedes it of rebuke and censure, by stating their obstinacy and their defiance toward the Messenger, following the statement of their stubborn refusal of the matter of reason (p-37). That is: by Allah, Aaron had indeed advised them and alerted them to the reality of the matter before Moses, peace be upon him, returned to them and addressed them with what was mentioned of the statements. It was also said: "before" refers to the words of the Samiri, as if he, peace be upon him, or when he saw him coming out of the pit, suspected that they had been seduced by him, so he hastened to warn them and said to them: ﴿O my people, you are only being tested by it﴾, that is: you have been put into temptation (fitna) by the calf, or you have been led astray by it, with the restrictive force (qasr) derived from the word "innama" directed to the act itself in comparison with its opposite, which they claim, and not to its stated qualifier in comparison with another qualifier, meaning: it is only that He has inflicted upon you temptation, not guidance to the truth; not in the sense that you were tested only by the calf and not by something else.

And His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful﴾, with the "inna" read with a kasra, coordinated with "innama", is guidance for them to the truth after restraining them from falsehood, and the mention of the title of Lordship and Mercy is for the sake of attending to winning them over to the truth, just as the mention of the description of the calf is for the sake of attending to restraining them from falsehood. That is: your Lord who deserves worship is the Most Merciful and no other. The "fa" in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿So follow me﴾ indicates the consequence of what follows it upon what precedes it of the content of the two clauses, that is: since the matter is such, then follow me in steadfastness upon the religion ﴿and obey my command﴾, this, and abandon the worship of what you have come to know its state.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 91:

﴿They said﴾ in answer to Harun, peace be upon him, ﴿"We will not cease to be devoted to it"﴾, to the calf and its worship, ﴿"staying [here] until Musa returns to us"﴾. They made his, peace be upon him, return to them the limit (ghayah) of their devotion to the worship of the calf; but not by way of a promise to abandon it upon his return, peace be upon him, rather by way of justification (ta'lil) and embellishment (taswiq). Beneath this they insinuated that he, peace be upon him, would not return with anything clear (mubin), relying on the saying of the Samiri. It is narrated that when they said this, Harun, peace be upon him, withdrew from them with twelve thousand, and they were the ones who had not worshipped the calf. When Musa, peace be upon him, returned and heard the shouting, and they were dancing around the calf, he said to the seventy who were with him, "This is the sound of fitna (trial, discord)," and he said to them what he said and heard from them what they said.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 92:

And His saying, ﴿Qala﴾ (He said), is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a sentence beginning a new thought) built upon a question that arose from the narration of their answer to Harun (peace be upon him). It is as if it were said: "What did Musa say to Harun, peace be upon them both, when he heard their answer to him, and did he approve of his silence after what he had witnessed from them?" So it was said: he said to him, while he was enraged, having seized his beard and head: ﴿O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray﴾ by worshipping the calf, and when they reached such obstinacy that they spoke to you with that abominable saying.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 93:

﴿Why do you not follow me?﴾ That is: "What prevented you from following me on the condition that you do not disapprove of it?" The second object of (manaʿa, "to prevent") is an object, and it governs "idh" (when). The meaning is: "What prevented you, at the time you saw their misguidance, from following me in zeal for God Most High and in fighting against those who disbelieved in Him?" It has also been said that the meaning is: "What compelled you not to follow me?", since preventing someone from something necessarily entails compelling them toward its opposite. It has also been said that the meaning is: "What prevented you from catching up with me and informing me of their misguidance, so that your departure from them would be a deterrent to them?" In this there is the point that the advice of Harun (peace be upon him), since they did not deter them from what they were upon, then his departing from them would be all the more so not a deterrent. The excuse that when they knew he would catch up with him and inform him of the story, they would fear Musa's (peace be upon him) return, and so they would refrain from that, is far from the realm of acceptance; how could it be, when they had declared that they would remain devoted to it until his (peace be upon him) return?

(p-38) ﴿Have you then disobeyed my command?﴾ That is: by firmness in the religion and defending it. For his (peace be upon them both) saying to him, "Take my place," definitively includes the command to do both of these, since succession is not realized except by the successor carrying out what the one who was succeeded would have carried out had he been present. The hamza is for reproachful denial, and the fa' is for coordination with an implied element required by the context, meaning: "Did you not follow me, or did you oppose me, so that you disobeyed my command?"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 94:

﴿He said: "O son of my mother!"﴾ He singled out "mother" for the attribution to magnify her right and to soften his heart, not because of what is said, that he was his brother on the mother's side, for the majority hold that the two were full brothers. ﴿Do not seize me by my beard nor by my head﴾, that is: nor by the hair of my head. It is narrated that he (peace be upon him) took the hair of his head with his right hand and his beard with his left, out of the intensity of his anger and the excess of his zeal for God. He (peace be upon him) was firm and unyielding in everything, so he could not contain himself when he saw them worshipping the calf, and he did what he did.

As for His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Indeed, I feared﴾ etc., it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to give the reason for the prohibition's ground by explaining the motive for abandoning fighting, and to establish that he was not disobeying his command but was in fact carrying it out. That is: I feared that if you fought them, some of them would fight others, they would annihilate one another and scatter.

﴿Lest you should say: "You have caused a division among the Children of Israel"﴾ by your own opinion, although they are sons of one father, as is indicated by their being mentioned under that title rather than "the people" or the like. By "division" he (peace be upon him) meant what fighting entails of a separation after which reunion is not to be hoped for.

﴿And you did not observe my word﴾. He means by this his saying (peace be upon him): ﴿Take my place among my people and set things right...﴾ etc., that is: I saw that the right course was to preserve the common folk and to be patient with them until you returned to them. Therefore I deferred to you so that you would be the one to manage the matter as you judged fit, especially since they were at the height of strength while we were few and weak, as His saying, exalted is He, expresses: ﴿Indeed, the people deemed me weak and nearly killed me﴾.

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) that comes as an answer to what arises from the narration of the earlier excuses of the people, who attributed the corruption to al-Samiri, and the excuse of Harun, peace be upon him. It is as if it were said: "What did Musa, peace be upon him, do after hearing what was related of the two excuses, and after the root of the trial was established against al-Samiri?" So it was said: he said, rebuking him, "This is their matter." ﴿So what is your business, O Samiri?﴾ That is: what is your situation, and what do you seek from what you have done? He, peace be upon him, addressed him this way so that he would expose to the people the falsehood of his scheme through his own confession, and so that he would deal with him, and with what he had made, with a punishment that would serve as a deterrent (*nakal*) for those who were tempted by it and for those nations that came after them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 96:

﴿He said﴾, that is, the Samiri, answering him, peace be upon him: ﴿I perceived what they did not perceive﴾ with a ḍammah on the ṣād in both words. It is also read with a kasrah on the ṣād in the first and a fatḥah in the second, and it is read with the tā' in both cases, addressing Moses, peace be upon him, and his people, meaning: I knew what the people did not know, and I grasped what they did not grasp, or I saw what they did not see. This last is the most fitting in light of what follows, His words: ﴿And thus my soul enticed me﴾, especially on the reading with the second person, for claiming knowledge of what Moses, peace be upon him, did not know is a great presumption that does not befit his station or his rank, unlike claiming to have seen what he did not see (p-39), peace be upon him, for that is among what happens by chance. He had seen that Gabriel, peace be upon him, had come riding a horse, and whenever the horse raised its forelegs or hind legs on the dry path, vegetation sprang up from beneath it at once. So he knew that it had a special status, and he took a handful from its footprint. This is His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿So I took a handful from the trace of the Messenger﴾. It is also read: "from the hoofprint of the horse of the Messenger", meaning: from the dust of the footprint of the horse of the angel who was sent to you to take you to the Mount. Perhaps mentioning him by the title of Messenger is to indicate his awareness of divine secrets that the people were not aware of, confirming what he opened his statement with, and alerting to the time at which he took what he took. ﴿Handful﴾ is the single instance of grasping, applied to what is grasped once. It is also read with a ḍammah on the qāf, which is the name of what is grasped, like ghurfah and muḍghah. It is also read: "fa-qabaṣtu qabṣah" with an unpointed ṣād, and the first is for taking with the whole palm, while the second is with the fingertips and the like, (as in) al-khaḍm and al-qaḍm. ﴿Then I threw it﴾, that is, into the melted ornaments, and so there came to be what came to be.

﴿And thus my soul enticed me﴾, that is, what I did of grasping and throwing. His words, exalted is He, "thus" (dhalika) are a reference to the verbal noun of the action mentioned after it, and the position of "thus" (kadhalika) is originally accusative, as a comparative verbal noun, that is, an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. The sense is: my soul enticed me with an enticement like that enticement. It was placed before the verb to convey restriction, and the kaf was regarded as superfluous to convey the emphasis of what the demonstrative conveyed of magnificence, so that it becomes the very emphasized verbal noun and not an adjective of it. That is: that wondrous adornment, my soul adorned for me what I did, and not any lesser adornment than it; and for that reason I did it. The gist of his answer is that what he did proceeded from him purely by following the desire of the soul that commands to evil and its seduction, not by anything else from rational proof or divine inspiration.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 97:

Then, at that point, ﴿he said﴾ (peace be upon him), ﴿"Go"﴾, i.e., away from among the people. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿"For it is yours in life to say, 'No touching'"﴾, etc., is a explanation of the consequence of the command. The "in" (fi) is connected to the stabilizing element (al-istiqrar) in "laka" (for you), meaning: it is established for you in life. Or it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) from the kaf (you), and the governing element is the sense of stabilization in the aforementioned adverbial phrase, because it depends on what is semantically the subject, not on His saying, exalted is He, ﴿"to say, 'No touching'"﴾, because of the presence of "anna" (that). That is: it is established for you, existing in life, i.e., for the duration of your life, that you separate from them with a complete separation, but not by way of choice in accordance with the obligation of legal responsibility, rather by way of compulsion that compels you to it. That is because God, exalted is He, struck him with an incurable disease, such that he could not touch anyone, nor could anyone, whoever they were, touch him without immediately developing a severe fever. So the people avoided him and kept away from him, and he would cry out with his utmost strength, "No touching." Meeting him, facing him, speaking with him, trading with him, and other dealings customarily carried out among people were forbidden to them, and he became more isolated among the people than a murderer who has taken refuge in the Sacred Precinct, and than a wild beast fleeing in the wilderness. It is said that his people still have this condition among them to this day. It was also read: "lā misās" like "fijār," and it is a proper name for the act of touching. Perhaps the secret of matching his offense with that particular punishment is the relation of opposition between them: since he initiated the trial by what his contact was a cause of the life of the dead, he was punished with its opposite, since his contact was made a cause of the fever, which is among the causes of the death of the living.

﴿"And indeed for you there is an appointment"﴾, i.e., in the Hereafter, ﴿"which you will not be able to break"﴾, i.e., God will not break that promise to you, but will certainly fulfill it for you after He has punished you in this world. It was read with a kasra on the lam, and the more apparent view is that it is from akhlaftu al-maw'id, i.e., I found it to be a fulfilled promise. It was also read with the nun (we) in quotation of the saying of the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿"And look at your god to which you were devoted, remaining in its worship"﴾, i.e., you remained steadfast in its worship, and the first lam was omitted for lightening. It was also read with a kasra on the zad by transferring the vowel of the lam to it.

﴿"We will surely burn it"﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, i.e., by fire. This is supported by the reading "lanuhrriqannahu" from burning (al-ihraq). It was said that it means by filing (al-mibrad), as an intensification of burning when it is filed with a file; and the reading "lanuharriqannahu" supports this.

﴿"Then We will surely scatter it"﴾, i.e., We will reduce it to dust, and it was read with a damma on the sin, ﴿"into the sea"﴾, as ashes or filings, as if it were dust.

﴿"in a scattering"﴾, such that no trace or remnant of it remains. Indeed, peace be upon him, did all of that, as the command to look at it testifies; and he did not state it explicitly, to draw attention to its complete manifestness and the impossibility of breaking His promise, which is confirmed by oath.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 98:

﴿Indeed, your god is only Allah﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) brought to establish the truth after refuting falsehood, by shifting the address and directing it to all. That is: indeed, your worshipped one who alone deserves worship is Allah ﴿Who there is no deity﴾ in existence for anything among things ﴿except Him﴾ alone, without anything sharing with Him in any way among the ways, of which are the attributes of divinity (ahkam al-uluhiyyah).

It is also read: "Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Most Merciful, Lord of the Throne."

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾, meaning: His knowledge has encompassed everything that is of the nature to be known. It is a substitute (badal) for the relative clause (silah), as if it were said: Indeed, your god is Allah, who has encompassed all things in knowledge, not other than Him, whatever it may be; thus the calf enters into this primarily. It is also read: "wasa'a" with the doubled letter (tashdid), in which case the accusative of "'ilman" (knowledge) is the object (maf'ulliyyah), because on the first reading it is truly the subject (fa'il). By transferring the verb to transitivity over two objects, the subject becomes the first object, as if it were said: His knowledge encompassed every thing. With this, the narration of Musa, peace be upon him, which is mentioned to establish the matter of tawhid (oneness of God), is complete, as its conclusion expresses.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary on surah 20, verse 99:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus do We relate to you﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*, a new sentence that begins anew and is not grammatically dependent on what precedes it). It is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ as a promise of goodness, that similar accounts of the bygone nations, like those already mentioned, will be sent down. "Thus" (*dhalika*) refers to the narrating of the story of Musa, peace be upon him, and the sense of distance in it is to announce his elevated rank and the great distance of his station in excellence. The *kaf* (in *kadhalika*) is in the accusative (*nasb*), on the basis that it is an adjective (*na't*) of an implied verbal noun (*masdar*). That is: We relate to you news of the past events that have already occurred, which befell the earlier nations, relating them in a manner like that relating which has passed. The fronting (of "thus") serves restriction (*qasr*), which conveys greater specification.

The *min* in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿of the news﴾ is in the accusative position. It is either the object of *naqussu* (we relate) considered in terms of its content, or it is connected to an implied element that is an adjective of the object, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and among us are those below that﴾, meaning: a group below that. The meaning is: We relate to you some of the news of what has already occurred, or some news that exists from among the news of what has already occurred. Its verification has already been discussed in the explanation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among the people is one who says...﴾ (2:8), etc. Its placement after "to you" is for the reason already mentioned many times: attention to what is put first and arousing eagerness for what is delayed. That is: like that excellent relating which you have heard, We relate to you what has been mentioned of the news, not a relating that falls short of it, as an insight for you, an augmentation of your knowledge, a multiplication of your miracles, and a reminder for those among your community who seek insight.

﴿And We have certainly given you from Us a reminder﴾, that is, a book containing these narratives and reports, worthy of reflection and taking lessons. The word "from" (*min*) is connected to "We have given you" (*ataynaka*). The indefiniteness of "a reminder" (*dhikran*) is for magnification. Its placement after the prepositional phrase is because the purpose of the statement lies in the fact that what is given is, from Him, Exalted is He, a great reminder and a noble Qur'an comprehensive of every perfection, not in the fact that this reminder is given from Him, Mighty and Majestic, together with what there is in it of a kind of length through the description that follows it. So fronting it would take away the splendor of the noble composition.

(p-41)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 100:

﴿Whoever turns away from it﴾ from that great Reminder, of supreme standing, which brings about the happiness of both abodes. It is also said: "from Allah, Mighty and Majestic." The "man" (من) here is either conditional (shart) or relative (mawsula), and in either case the clause is a description (sifa) of dhikran (Reminder).

﴿Then indeed he﴾ that is, the one who turns away from it, ﴿will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden (wizr)﴾ that is, a heavy, crushing punishment for his disbelief and all his other sins. Calling it "wizr" is either because of its resemblance, in the heaviness it places on the one punished and the difficulty of bearing it, to a load that weighs down the carrier and breaks his back, or because it is the recompense of the wizr, which is sin. The first is more fitting in light of what follows, where it is called a load (himl).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 101:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿abiding therein﴾ — that is, in the burden, or in its enduring bearing — is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun concealed in "yaḥmilu" (he bears). The plural is used with regard to the meaning of "man" (man), since abiding forever in the Fire is something that is realized when its people are gathered together, just as the singular is used in the three pronouns mentioned earlier, with regard to its wording.

﴿And evil it is for them on the Day of Resurrection as a burden﴾ — that is, "wretched is it for them." In it there is an ambiguous pronoun (ḍamīr mubham) which is explained by "as a burden" (ḥimlan), and the thing being specified by the dispraise (al-makhsūs bi-l-dhamm) is omitted, that is: "evil as a burden is their load." The lam (la-hum) is for clarification (lil-bayan), as in ﴿Hayta laka﴾ (Qur'an 12:23, "Come, you"), as if, when it was said, "evil it is," it was asked, "for whom is this said?" and so the answer was given: "for them." The repetition of "the Day of Resurrection" is for the increase of affirmation (taqrir) and the magnifying of the matter (tahwil al-amr).

﴿Yawma yunfakhu fi al-ṣūr﴾ (the Day when the Trumpet is blown) is a *badal* (substitute, in grammatical apposition) for "the Day of Resurrection." Alternatively, it is in the accusative by an implied verb, *udhkur* ("remember"), or it is an adverbial complement (*ẓarf*) of a verb that has been omitted. The omission is made to signal that the expression is too narrow to contain and explain it, as was explained earlier in the commentary on His words, ﴿The Day when Allah gathers the Messengers﴾, and His words, ﴿The Day We shall gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾.

It has also been read as *nanfukhu* (with the nūn, "We blow"), attributing the blowing to the One who commands it, to honour it. It has also been read with an open *yāʾ* (*yanfukhu*, "He blows"), with the pronoun referring either to Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, or to Isrāfīl, peace be upon him, even though he has not been mentioned, because he is well known.

﴿And We shall gather the guilty that Day﴾ means: on the Day when the Trumpet is blown. The explicit mention of it, although it is clear that gathering will only take place on that Day, is for the sake of inspiring awe. It has also been read *wa-yuḥsharu al-mujrimūna* ("and the guilty will be gathered").

﴿Blue-eyed﴾ means: their eyes will be blue. They are described thus because blueness is the worst colour of the eye and the most hateful to the Arabs. The Romans, who were the greatest of their enemies, were blue-eyed, and for this reason they described the enemy as "black-livered, red-bearded, and blue-eyed." Or it may mean "blind," because the pupil of the blind man turns blue.

The Exalted said: ﴿They will whisper among themselves﴾, meaning: they will lower and conceal their voices, because of the terror and dread that fill their hearts. It is a resumptive clause explaining what they will say and do at that time, or it is another circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the criminals, meaning: some of them will say to others, in a whisper: ﴿You did not remain﴾, meaning: you did not remain in the world, ﴿except ten﴾, meaning: ten nights, belittling the duration of their stay there because it has passed away; or they regard the duration of the Hereafter as long; or it is due to their regret over it when they witness the hardships and become certain that they deserve them for having wasted it on fulfilling desires and following appetites. Or the verse refers to "in the moon," which is the most fitting for their state, for when they witness the resurrection that they used to deny in the world and regarded as impossible, they cannot help but say that, acknowledging it and affirming how swiftly it has come about, as if they were saying: "You have been raised, and you did not remain in the grave except a short period." Otherwise, their condition is too dreadful for them to be occupied with recalling the days of blessing and joy, belittling them, and lamenting over them.

﴿We know best what they say﴾, namely the length of their stay. ﴿When their most upright in course says﴾, that is, the most just of them in opinion or conduct, ﴿"You stayed only a day"﴾. Attributing this statement to the most upright of them is a retraction (istirja') by Him, exalted is He, of it; yet not because it is closer to truth, but because it better demonstrates the intensity of the terror.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 105:

﴿They ask you about the mountains.﴾ That is: about the final outcome of their matter (ma'al amrihā). A man from Thaqif asked about this, and it is said: the polytheists of Mecca asked it in a spirit of mockery.

﴿Say: My Lord will scatter them, scattering.﴾ That is: He will make them like sand, then send winds over them that will disperse them. The fa' (the particle "fa," here indicating immediacy) is for hastening to silence the questioners.

﴿So He will leave it﴾ The pronoun may refer to the mountains, taking into account their remaining parts after being blown away, namely their places and bases; that is, He will leave what has spread out of them, its surface made level with the surfaces of all other parts of the earth, after the blowing away of what had jutted out and risen up from them. Or it may refer to the earth, which is implied by the context, since it is what remains after the mountains are blown away. On both interpretations, He leaves the whole.

﴿a level plain, smooth﴾ Because when the mountains are leveled and their surface is made equal to the surfaces of all other parts of the earth, the whole becomes one surface. The qā' (قاع) has been said to mean the plain; it has been said to mean the uncovered part of the earth; it has been said to mean the solid level part of it; and it has been said to mean that in which there is neither plant nor building. The ṣafṣaf (صفصف) is the level, smooth ground, as though its parts were a single row on every side. The accusative of "qā'an" (قاعًا) is either as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the accusative pronoun, or it is a second object of "yadhar" (يذر) with the meaning of "making" (taḍmīn al-taṣyīr) being implied. "Ṣafṣafan" (صفصفًا) is either a second circumstantial state, or an apposition (badal) to the second object.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 107:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You will not see therein﴾, i.e., the resting places of the mountains, or in the earth according to what has passed of the detail, ﴿any crookedness [ʿiwaja]﴾ with the ʿayn vowelled with a kasra (ʿiwaj), i.e., any bending whatsoever, which, due to its extreme subtlety, is like the matters of meanings (min qabil ma fi al-maʿani), i.e., you will not perceive it if you examine it with geometrical measures (al-maqayis al-handasiyya).

﴿Nor any elevation [amta]﴾, i.e., a slight protrusion. This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the manner of what preceded regarding the level plain (al-qaʿ al-safsaf), or it is another circumstantial clause (hal), or it is an attributive (sifa) to qaʿan. The address is to everyone from whom sight can come. The fronting of the prepositional phrase over the explicit object is, as has been mentioned many times, for the sake of emphasis on what is fronted and to create anticipation for what is delayed, together with the length that might be disrupted by fronting it, which could impair the harmonious interlinking of the parts of the noble composition.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 108:

﴿That day﴾ i.e., the day when the mountains are blown away, with the day being attributed to the time of the blowing, and it is an adverbial complement (zarf) for the words of the Exalted: ﴿they will follow the caller﴾. It has also been said that it is a substitute (badal) for "the Day of Resurrection," but this is not so. That is, the people will follow the caller of God, Mighty and Majestic, to the place of assembly (mahshar), and he is Israfil, upon him be peace, who calls the people at the second blast (al-nafkhah al-thaniyah), standing upon the rock of Jerusalem, and says: "O decayed bones, scattered joints and torn flesh, gather to the presentation before the All-Merciful," and they will come from every direction toward Him.

﴿No crookedness will there be for him﴾ No one summoned will deviate for him, nor will anyone turn away from him.

﴿And voices will be hushed before the All-Merciful﴾ i.e., they will be humbled by His awe, ﴿so you will hear nothing but a whisper﴾ i.e., a faint sound. From this comes hamis (a faint sound), used for the sound of camels' feet; and the whisper has been explained as the sound of their feet striking the ground as they are led to the place of assembly.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 109:

﴿On that day﴾, i.e., the day on which the terrifying matters mentioned will take place, ﴿intercession will not benefit﴾ anyone from the intercessors, ﴿except for one whom the Most Merciful has permitted﴾ to intercede for him, ﴿and whose word He approves﴾. That is, He approves the words of the intercessor concerning his case, or He approves his (the intercessor's) words for the sake of the one interceded for and concerning him. As for anyone other than him, intercession hardly benefits him, even if it is supposed to come from the intercessors who take it upon themselves to intercede for people, as in His saying, ﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them﴾. Thus the exception, as you see, is from the most general of the objects (al-mafa'il, i.e., the grammatical objects). As for its being an exception from "intercession," in the sense of "intercession will not benefit except the intercession of one whom the Most Merciful has permitted to intercede for another," as some have allowed, there is no way to accept it, because the ruling on intercession regarding one who has not been permitted is that he does not possess it, and it does not proceed from him at all, as in His saying, ﴿They do not possess intercession, except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾, and His saying, ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾. So reporting about it merely by the absence of its benefit to the one interceded for may give the false impression that it could proceed from one who has not been permitted, while also failing to fulfill the requirement of the context of describing the terror of that day. As for His saying, ﴿And no intercession from it will be accepted﴾, its meaning is the absence of permission for intercession, not the absence of its acceptance after it has taken place.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 110:

﴿He knows what is before them﴾ i.e., the circumstances that preceded them. It is also said: it refers to the matters of this world.

﴿And what is behind them﴾ and what comes after them of what they will face. It is also said: it refers to the matters of the Hereafter.

﴿And they do not encompass Him in knowledge﴾ i.e., their knowledge does not encompass His known objects, may He be exalted. It is also said: it refers to His essence, meaning in terms of His being characterized by the attributes of perfection, among which is all-encompassing knowledge. It is also said: the pronoun refers to one of the two relative clauses (i.e., "what is before them" or "what is behind them"), or to both of them together, for they do not know all of that nor the details of what they know of it.

I need to translate carefully, keeping Qur'anic quotations in ﴿ ﴾ with plain meaning, transliterating technical terms with glosses on first use, and rendering the hadith/athar and grammar points faithfully.

Translation:

﴿And faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all.﴾ That is: they will be abased and will submit with the submission of the rebellious, i.e., the captives in the hand of the Irresistible King. Perhaps these are the faces of the criminals, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Evil will be the faces of those who disbelieved﴾. And it is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he has failed who carries injustice﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "He has lost who associated partners with Allah and did not repent." This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the reason their faces were humbled, or an interjection (i'tirad), as if it were said: "They failed and lost." It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to "the faces." The word "man" (من) is an expression referring to them, serving in place of its pronoun. It has also been said that "the faces" is general in meaning, so the sense then is: "And he has failed, from among them, who carried injustice."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 112:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds﴾ and so on, is a continuation (qasam) of His saying, may He be exalted, "And he has indeed failed who bears wrongdoing (zulman)," and not of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And the faces will be humbled﴾ and so on. Likewise it is so according to the first aspect (wajh), meaning: and whoever does some of the righteous deeds, or some portion of the righteous deeds, according to one of the two aspects mentioned in the interpretation of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿from the news of what has passed before﴾.

﴿And he is a believer﴾, for faith (iman) is a condition for the validity of acts of obedience (ta'at) and the acceptance of good deeds (hasanat). ﴿So he will not fear injustice﴾, that is, the withholding of a reward that is due by the binding force of the promise.

﴿Nor﴾ (p-44) ﴿diminution﴾, nor any breaking off from it that would reduce it. Or the meaning is: he does not fear the requital of injustice and diminution, when no injustice or diminution has proceeded from him, so that he would fear either of them. It has also been read: "fa-la yakhaf" (so let him not fear), as a prohibition (nahy).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 113:

﴿And thus﴾ is conjoined to ﴿Thus do We relate﴾, and "that" (dhalika) is a reference to the sending down of the preceding verses, which contain the threats scattered about what will happen of the states of the Resurrection and its terrors; i.e., "like that sending down."

﴿We have sent it down﴾, i.e., the whole Qur'an, and its being referred to by a pronoun without prior mention is to signal the eminence of its matter and that it is firmly fixed in minds and present in intellects.

﴿As an Arabic Qur'an﴾, so that the Arabs may understand it and comprehend the inimitable composition (nazm) in it, which indicates that it lies beyond the capacity of humans and was sent down from the One who creates the powers and decrees.

﴿And We have varied in it of the threats﴾, i.e., We have repeated in it some of the threats, or some of the threats as has been indicated just above.

﴿That they may fear God﴾, i.e., that they may actually guard themselves against disbelief and sins.

﴿Or it may create for them a remembrance﴾, i.e., an admonition and a lesson that leads, in the end, to guarding oneself.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 114:

﴿So exalted is Allah﴾: an expression of magnification of Him, the Exalted, and of His affairs by which He directs His servants through commands and prohibitions, promise and threat, and other things. That is: He is elevated in His essence and transcendent above resembling created beings in His essence, attributes, actions and states.

﴿The King﴾: whose command and prohibition are executed, and who is worthy that His promise be hoped for and His threat be feared.

﴿The Truth﴾: in His dominion and divinity, by virtue of His essence; or, the one who is established in His essence and attributes.

﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation (wahy) is completed for you﴾: that is, before ﴿its revelation﴾ is finished. When Jibril, upon him be peace, would convey the revelation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he would follow it at the pronunciation of every letter and every word, out of his complete eagerness to receive it and to memorize it. So he was forbidden from this, following the mention of the sending down, by way of digression, since the fixing of words in minds follows the fixing of their meanings in them, and pronouncing one word may occupy one from hearing what follows it. He was commanded to seek the abundance of knowledge and to request more of it from Allah, the Exalted, so it was said: ﴿And say﴾, that is, within yourself: ﴿My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾, that is: ask Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for an increase in knowledge, for it is what leads to your goal without haste. It was also said that he was forbidden from conveying what was still unclear before its explanation came; but this is not so, for conveying and reciting the unclear before its explanation is something about whose soundness and legitimacy there is no doubt.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 115:

﴿And We certainly made a covenant with Adam﴾ is a resumptive statement (kalam musta'naf), brought to establish what preceded of the varied threats in the Qur'an, and to explain that the foundation of the children of Adam is on disobedience and their root is firmly fixed in forgetfulness. It also fulfils the promise in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus do We relate to you some of the news of what has passed﴾. It is said: "'ahida ilayhi al-malik," "'azama 'alayhi," and "taqaddama ilayhi," when he commanded him and enjoined him. The object (al-ma'hud, the covenanted matter) is omitted, indicated by what follows it. The lam is the answer to an omitted oath, meaning: "And I swear," or "By God," or "By God indeed, We certainly commanded him and enjoined him."

﴿from before﴾, i.e., from before this time. ﴿so he forgot﴾, i.e., the covenant, and did not attend to it until he became heedless of it, or he abandoned it as one who has forgotten it. It is also read "fanussiya," i.e., the Satan caused him to forget.

﴿and We did not find in him resolve﴾: determination of opinion and firmness of foot in matters. For if he had possessed that, Satan would not have made him slip, nor would he have been able to deceive him. This was from him, peace be upon him, at the beginning of his affair, before he had tested matters, experienced their heat and cold, and tasted their bitterness and sweetness. From the Prophet (ﷺ): "If the forbearance (ahlam) of the children of Adam were weighed against the forbearance of Adam, his forbearance would outweigh it." And God Most High has said: ﴿and We did not find in him resolve﴾. It is said: resolve over the sin, for he erred and did not intend it. As for His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and We did not find﴾: if it is from existence in the sense of knowledge (wujud 'ilmi), then "lahu 'azman" is a double object, and the second (the prepositional phrase "lahu") is placed before the first ("'azman") because it is an adverbial complement (zarf). If it is from existence in the sense opposite to non-existence (wujud muqabil lil-'adam), which is the more appropriate reading, because the point of the statement lies in the object, and there is no special merit in informing that the resolve which was absent belongs to him, then "lahu" is connected to the verb and placed before its object ("'azman") for the reason mentioned many times before, namely emphasis on the fronted element and creating suspense for what is delayed. Alternatively, it is connected to an omitted element which is a circumstantial complement (hal) of its indefinite object ("'azman"), as if it were said: "and We did not encounter for him resolve."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 116:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [remember] when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾ begins the explanation of what was previously known (al-ma'hud) and of how his forgetfulness became apparent and his resolve was lost. "Idh" (when) is in the accusative as an object of an implied verb addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: "And remember the time when We said to them." Linking the remembrance to a time, although the intended meaning is to remind of the events that occurred in it, is due to what has been repeatedly mentioned regarding the emphasis on the obligation of remembering them. The time encompasses the details of the matters that occurred in it, so the command to remember it is a command, by way of demonstrative proof, to remember the details of what occurred in it. Also, because the time encompasses the actual events, when it is mentioned the events become as if they exist in the mind of the addressee with their concrete existences. That is: "Remember what occurred in that time from Us and from him, until it becomes clear to you that he forgot and lost his resolve."

﴿So they prostrated, except Iblis﴾ The discussion of this has already preceded several times.

﴿He refused﴾ is a resumptive sentence that came as an answer to a question arising from the report of his not prostrating, as if it were said: "What is the matter with him that he did not prostrate?" So it was said: "He refused and was arrogant." The object of "abā" (refused) is either omitted, meaning: "He refused the prostration," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He refused to be among those who prostrate﴾, or it is not intended at all, by treating it as an intransitive verb, meaning: he performed refusal and manifested it.

﴿So We said﴾ immediately after that, out of care for his counsel, ﴿O Adam, indeed this﴾ one, whose deed you have seen, ﴿is an enemy to you and to your spouse. So let him not drive you both out﴾, that is, let him not become a cause of your expulsion ﴿from the Garden﴾. The intended meaning is a prohibition against placing yourselves in a state where Satan could find a way to expel you from it by a demonstrative (burhani) method, as in your saying: "Let me not see you here." The particle الفاء (fa’) indicates that the prohibition follows from his enmity toward them, or from the report of it. ﴿Then you will be wretched﴾ is the answer to the prohibition. Attributing wretchedness to him alone, after making the expulsion, which necessitates it, dependent on both of them together, is because he is the origin in affairs, and because his wretchedness entails hers, along with the consideration of the fawasil (the rhyming verse-endings). It has been said that the intended wretchedness is the toil involved in obtaining the means of livelihood, and that this is among the duties of men.

﴿Indeed, for you there is that you will not hunger therein, nor be unclothed﴾ ﴿and that you will not thirst therein, nor be exposed to the sun﴾. This is a *ta'lil* (a stated reason, justification) for what the prohibition requires. The gathering of the causes of comfort therein necessitates exaggerated concern in securing the foundations of remaining there, and earnestness in avoiding whatever would lead to leaving it. It also explains the avoidance of explicitly stating that for him (ﷺ)... [Note: the text reads "عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ", rendered as follows:] for him, peace be upon him, there is enjoyment of various kinds of blessings in food and drink, and delight in kinds of fine clothing and pleasing dwellings. Although there is in this, of encouragement to remain there, what is not hidden, the mention of negating its opposites, which are hunger, thirst, nakedness and sun-exposure, serves to remind of those disagreeable matters and to alert to the kinds of wretchedness in them, against which he was warned, so that he would greatly guard against the cause that leads to them. Moreover, encouragement has been achieved by what was permitted to him of enjoying everything therein except what was excepted regarding the tree, as expressed by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And O Adam, dwell you and your wife in the Garden, and eat from it freely wherever you wish﴾ [2:35]. Its mention is omitted here, being sufficed by what was mentioned in another place, and he limited himself to the encouragement which includes the warning.

The meaning of ﴿that you will not hunger therein...﴾ and so on is that none of the four matters befalls him at all. Satiety, quenching, clothing and shelter may be obtained after their opposites have appeared, through lack of food, drink, clothing and dwelling. That is not the case there. Rather, whatever desire or inclination arises therein toward any of the mentioned matters is enjoyed without reaching the point of necessity.

The reason for singling him out with what was mentioned is what has just passed. Thirst is separated from hunger in the mention, despite their homogeneity and their customary juxtaposition in speech, and likewise the case of nakedness and sun-exposure, which are homogeneous. This fulfils the station of favour its due by indicating that the negation of each one of these matters is a blessing in its own right. Had hunger and thirst been combined, it might have been thought that negating them is one single blessing. The same applies to combining nakedness and sun-exposure, following the manner of the story of the cow. To further affirm, by alerting that the negation of each of the mentioned matters is intended in itself and mentioned primarily, and not that the negation of some is mentioned incidentally (*istitrad*) and subordinately to the negation of another, as might be imagined if each of the two homogeneous pairs were combined.

It is read ﴿إنَّكَ﴾ with a kasra (*inna-ka*), while the majority read it with a fatha (*anna-ka*), coordinated with ﴿أن لا تجوع﴾ (that you not hunger). The validity of the clause beginning with the fathah-form *anna* as the subject of the kasra-form *inna* (which shares its function of emphasis) is as follows. Although the clause cannot be the predicate of *inna* (because of the prohibition against two emphasis particles occurring in one construction), there is no such combination here, since the scope of emphasis differs between the two. This is unlike when it is the predicate of *inna*, where unity of scope is undoubtedly present. Explanation: each of *inna* (with kasra) and *anna* (with fatha) is set to affirm the content of a declarative clause formed of its subject and predicate. The declarative nature of such a clause lies in the positive or negative judgment it contains, and the locus of that judgment is its predicate, not its subject. So the meaning of each is the affirmation that its predicate holds of its subject, not the affirmation of its subject in itself. Therefore, what follows from a clause introduced by fathah-*anna* as the subject of kasra-*inna* is the affirmation of the predicate's holding of that clause, which is interpreted as a verbal noun. The affirmation of the subject in itself is necessarily the meaning of the fathah-form, so there is definitively no combination of two emphasis particles in one construction. The scholars did not permit saying *inna anna Zaydan qa'imun haqq* (with the scope differing), but required separation by a predicate, as in our saying *inna 'indi anna Zaydan qa'im* (indeed, with me it is that Zayd is standing), to avoid the appearance of combination. The conjunctive *wa* (and), although it stands in for the kasra-particle, which cannot precede the fathah-particle without separation, and takes its place in conveying its meaning and applying its rulings to what follows it, is not itself a particle set for emphasis. Therefore, its prefixing to the fathah-form does not entail the combination of two emphasis particles at all.

The meaning is: for you is the absence of hunger, the absence of nakedness, and the absence of thirst. However, he did not limit himself to stating that what is established for him (peace be upon him) is the absence of thirst and sun-exposure absolutely, as was done with the coordinated item (the preceding clause). Rather, the intention is to state that what is established for him (peace be upon him) is the affirmation of their absence. So it is placed in the position of the verbal particle *anna*, the one protected and reinforced, which conveys this, as if it were said: for you therein is the absence of your thirst with certainty.
