Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 120:

﴿Then Satan whispered to him.﴾ That is: he conveyed his whispering to him, or he confided it to him. ﴿He said﴾ — either it is a substitute (badal) for "whispered," or it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that came as an answer to a question arising from it, as if it were said: "What did he say in his whispering?" So it was said: he said: ﴿"O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity (shajarat al-khuld)?"﴾ That is: a tree whoever eats from it is made eternal and never dies at all, whether he remains in his state or becomes a king, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Except that you become two angels or become of the immortals."﴾

﴿And a kingdom that does not decay.﴾ That is: one that does not cease, and is not corrupted in any way whatsoever.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 121:

﴿So they both ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: They were stripped of the light with which Allah, Exalted, had clothed them, until their private parts became exposed.

﴿And they began to fasten over themselves some leaves of the Garden﴾. Its explanation has already passed in (Surah al-A'raf).

﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord﴾ by what he had mentioned of eating from the tree, ﴿so he went astray﴾: he strayed from his objective, which is immortality, or from the command given to him, or from right guidance, in that he was deceived by the words of the enemy. It has also been read as "fa-ghawi" (fa-ghawiya), from ghawiya al-fasil, meaning when the young camel has overeaten from milk. The description of him, peace be upon him, with disobedience and error, despite the smallness of his lapse, is an exaltation of it and a forceful warning to his offspring against the like of it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 122:

﴿Then his Lord chose him﴾, i.e., He selected him, brought him near to Himself, and inclined him to repentance and granted him success in it. The verb is from ijtaba (to choose, to gather to oneself) in the sense of jaba, i.e., he gathered it for himself, meaning he collected it, as in your saying "ijtama'tuhu" (I gathered it); or from "jaba ila ka dhā fa-ijtabaytuhu" (he brought such-and-such to me, so I gathered it), like "jalīb 'ala al-'arūs fa-ijtalaytuhā" (a bride's escort brought to the bride, so I unveiled her). The root meaning of the word is gathering. Mentioning the title of Lordship (rububiyya) together with the attachment to his pronoun, peace be upon him, is an additional honouring of him, peace be upon him.

﴿Then He accepted his repentance﴾, i.e., He accepted his repentance when he and his wife repented, saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾. The reason for singling him out, peace be upon him, for choosing and acceptance of repentance has already been explained.

﴿And guided him﴾, i.e., to steadfastness upon repentance and holding fast to the means of protection (ʿiṣma).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 123:**

﴿Said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), built upon a question that arises from the report that Allah, exalted is He, accepted his repentance and guided him. It is as if it were said: "What did Allah, exalted is He, command him after that?" So it is said: He said to him and to his wife: ﴿Go down from it, all of you﴾, i.e., descend from the Garden to the earth. The words of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿some of you are enemies to others﴾ are a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun of address in "go down" (ihbitā). The plural is used because they are the origin of the offspring and the source of the children; that is, they are hostile to one another in matters of livelihood, as is the case among people in terms of mutual pulling and fighting.

﴿Then if there comes to you guidance from Me﴾ through a Book and a Messenger, ﴿whoever follows My guidance﴾: the apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun, together with its attribution to His pronoun, exalted is He, in order to honour it and to emphasise the obligation of following it.

﴿Then he will not go astray﴾ in this world, ﴿nor will he be distressed﴾ in the Hereafter.(p-48)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 124:

﴿And whoever turns away from My remembrance﴾ i.e., from the guidance that reminds of Me and calls to Me, ﴿indeed for him is﴾ in this world ﴿a constricted life﴾, ḍankan (narrow, constricted), a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as an adjective, which is why it applies equally to the masculine and the feminine. It is also read ḍankā, like sakrā, because the focus of his aspiration and the aim of his gaze are confined to the material goods of this world; he is consumed by their increase and fearful of their decrease. This is unlike the believer who seeks the Hereafter, although God may constrict [the life] of the believer on account of the ill effect of disbelief, and expand it through the blessing of faith, as He said, the Exalted: ﴿And humiliation and wretchedness were struck upon them﴾. And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful [of God], We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾. And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed﴾ up to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾. It is said: it is ḍarī' and zaqqūm in the Fire; and it is said: it is the punishment of the grave.

﴿And We will raise him﴾ It is also read with the ha' vowelless, following the pausal form, and with jazm (the apocopate), in conjunction with the grammatical position (maḥall) of fa-inna lahu ma'īshatan ḍankan, since it is the response of the conditional.

﴿on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾ bereft of sight, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute and deaf﴾, not blind to the proof, as has been said.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 125:

﴿He says﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), as has been explained earlier. ﴿My Lord, why have You raised me up blind, when I was sighted?﴾ That is, in the worldly life. It is also read "a'mā" with imalah (the vowel-raising of alif toward i) in both places, and in the first place only, because it is the proper place for alteration, being the end of the verse and the place of pause (waqf).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 126:

﴿He said: "Thus"﴾ i.e., just like that did you act. Then he explained it with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Our signs came to you﴾, clear and luminous, such that they are hidden from no one, ﴿but you forgot them﴾, i.e., you became blind to them and abandoned them in the manner of one who is forgotten and not remembered at all. ﴿And thus﴾, in the same way, ﴿that forgetting which you practised in the world, today you will be forgotten﴾, left in blindness and punishment as a recompense in kind (jaza' wifaqan). ﴿But not forever, as it has been said; rather, for as long as God wills,﴾ then He removes it from him, so he sees the terrors of the Resurrection and witnesses his place in the Fire, and that will be a punishment for him over and above the punishment. Likewise, God, the Exalted, removes from them dumbness and deafness: ﴿Hear them and see them on the day they come to Us﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 127:

﴿And thus﴾ i.e., like that recompense, which corresponds to the transgression, ﴿We recompense him who transgresses﴾ by being immersed in the desires, ﴿and does not believe in the signs of his Lord﴾ rather he denied them and turned away from them, ﴿and the punishment of the Hereafter﴾ in absolute terms, or the punishment of the Fire, ﴿is severer and more lasting﴾ i.e., than the straitness of living, or than that together with the gathering blind (on the Day of Resurrection).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 128:**

﴿Has it not become clear to them how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ This is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʼnaf), brought in to confirm what precedes it, namely His words: ﴿And thus do We recompense...﴾ to the end of the verse. The hamza (al-hamza) is for reproachful denial (al-inkar al-tawbikhi), and the fa' is for coordination (al-ʻatf) with an implied element required by the context. The use of the verb hada (guidance, "to show/make clear") with the preposition lam (lahum, "for them") is either because it has been treated as if it were transitive by the lam itself, so there is no need for an object (al-maf'ul), or because it carries the sense of "making clear" (al-tabyin), with the object omitted. Whichever is the case, the subject (al-fa'il) is the clause together with what it governs, and its meaning. The pronoun in "lahum" refers to the polytheists contemporary with the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The meaning is: they were heedless, so the guidance was not made for them; or, so it was not made clear to them what the outcome of their affair would be, given how many of the former generations We destroyed. This has already been mentioned in His words: ﴿Has it not become clear to those who inherit the land after its former people...﴾ (Qur'an 7:100). It has been said that the subject is the pronoun referring to God, Exalted and Majestic, and the reading with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azama) supports this.

As for His words, ﴿How many We destroyed...﴾ to the end, it is either a clause suspending the verb (mu'allaq li-l-fi'l) that takes the place of its object, or it explains an omitted object. This is what has been said. The more probable view is that no object should be assumed for it, as if it were said: "Did God, Exalted, not make guidance clear to them?" Then, by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), it is said: ﴿How many We destroyed...﴾ to the end, as an explanation of that guidance. The phrase ﴿from the generations﴾ (min al-qurun) is in the accusative position as a qualifier of its specifier (mumayyiz), i.e., "how many generations, being among the generations."

His words ﴿walking in their dwellings﴾ (yamshuna fi masakinihim) are a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the generations," or from the object of "We destroyed," meaning: We destroyed them while they were in a state of security and moving about in their homes. Or it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "lahum," emphasizing the reproach, and the governing element is "yuhda" (it becomes clear). The meaning is: has it not become clear to them that Our destruction of the earlier generations, the companions of al-Hijr, Thamud, and the cities of the people of Lut, is something they witness, as they walk in their dwellings when they travel to al-Sham, observing the traces of their destruction? That in itself necessitates that they be guided to the truth and take warning, lest there befall them the like of what befell those. It has been read as yamshuna in the passive voice (al-bina' lil-maf'ul), meaning: they are enabled to walk.

﴿Indeed in that﴾ (inna fi dhalika) is a justification for the reproach and a confirmation that guidance was there even though they did not heed it. "That" (dhalika) is a reference to the content of His words ﴿How many We destroyed...﴾ to the end. The distal form, with the sense of distance, indicates the elevated status of that matter and the greatness of its importance in its own domain. ﴿There are signs﴾ (la-ayatin), many, great, clearly guiding and manifestly indicating the truth. Therefore they were guided most completely (hadaw ayyama hadaw). It is permissible that the particle "fi" (in) be abstractive (tajridiyya), so reflect upon this. ﴿For people of understanding﴾ (li-uli al-nuha), for those with intellects that restrain from ugly deeds, among the worst of which is what the disbelievers of Makkah engage in: denial of the signs of God, Exalted, turning a blind eye to them, and other kinds of disobedience. There is in this an indication that the content of the clause is the subject (al-fa'il), not the object (al-maf'ul).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 129:**

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾ is a new sentence (*kalam mustaʾnaf*), brought to explain the wisdom behind the non-occurrence of what his statement, the Exalted, ﴿"Has it not guided them..."﴾ and so on, the verse, implies: that they would be struck by the like of what befell the generations that were destroyed. That is: had it not been for the preceding word, namely the promise to delay the punishment of this nation until the Hereafter, for a wisdom that requires it and a benefit that calls for it.

﴿would have been⁠﻿ the punishment for their misdeeds⁠﻿ ﴾ *lizaman* (inseparable, binding), meaning necessarily binding upon these disbelievers, such that it would not be delayed from their misdeeds even for an hour, in the way that what befell those who passed before them was binding. In the use of the title of Lordship (*rububiyya*) together with its addition to his pronoun, peace be upon him, there is an allusion that this delay is for his honour, peace be upon him, as his statement, the Exalted, indicates: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾. *Al-lizam* is either a verbal noun (*masdar*) of *lazima*, described by it for emphasis, or a form (*fiʿal*) with the meaning of *mifʿal*, made into the instrument of binding because of its intense binding quality, as it is said *lizaz khasm* (the tenacious adversary).

﴿and a specified term⁠﻿ ﴾ is conjoined to "word" (*kalima*), that is: and had it not been for a specified term for their lifetimes, or for their punishment, which is the Day of Resurrection and the Day of Badr, their punishment would not have been delayed at all. He separated it from what it is conjoined to in order to hasten to explain the answer to "had it not been" (*lawla*), and to indicate the independence of each of the two in negating the necessity of punishment, and to observe the rhyming endings of the noble verses. It has also been permitted to conjoin it to the concealed pronoun in "would have been" (*kana*), which refers to the immediate seizure understood from the context, treating the separation by the predicate as equivalent to emphasis. That is: the immediate seizure and a specified term would have been binding upon them, like the case of ʿAd, Thamud (p-50) and their like. The specified term alone did not stand apart from the immediate seizure.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 130:

﴿So be patient over what they say.﴾ That is: since the matter is as has been mentioned, that the delay of their punishment is not neglect but respite, and that it is certainly binding upon them. ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾ of the words of disbelief. Indeed, his knowledge (peace be upon him) that they will certainly be punished is something that consoles him and moves him to patience.

﴿And glorify﴾ while joining ﴿the praise of your Lord﴾. That is: pray while you are praising your Lord, who has brought you to perfection through His guidance and success; or, declare Him far above what they attribute to Him of things that do not befit His exalted majesty, while praising Him for having distinguished you with guidance and acknowledging that He is the source of all blessings. The first is the more evident and fits His saying, exalted is He: ﴿before the rising of the sun﴾, etc., for specifying a time for glorification is not customary. Thus what is meant is the dawn prayer (Salat al-Fajr).

﴿And before its setting﴾ means: the prayers of noon (Zuhr) and afternoon (Asr), because they fall before its setting and after its decline; and he gathered them to match His saying, exalted is He: ﴿before the rising of the sun﴾, and before the afternoon prayer (Asr).

﴿And during the hours of the night﴾ means: from its periods; the plural of ʾinan (إنى), with a kasra and shortened vowel, and ʾana'a (آناء), with a fatha and lengthened vowel.

﴿So glorify﴾ means: so pray. What is meant by it is the evening prayer (Maghrib) and the night prayer (Isha'), and the mention of the time in these two is because they are distinguished by greater excellence, for the heart is most gathered in them and the soul is most inclined to rest, so worship in them is more arduous. For this reason, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the rising of the night is more firm in tread and more upright in speech.﴾

﴿And the extremes of the day﴾ is a repetition for the dawn and the Maghrib prayers, as an indication that these two are distinguished by a greater excellence. Its coming in the plural form is because there is no confusion; like the saying of one who said: "Its two backs are like the backs of two shields." Or it may refer to the command to pray the noon prayer, for it is the end of the first half of the day and the beginning of the last half, and its plural is in consideration of the two halves. Or because "day" is a genus noun. Or it is a command to voluntary prayer in parts of the day.

﴿That perhaps you may be pleased﴾ is connected to "glorify": that is, glorify during these times in hope that you may attain from Him, exalted is He, that with which your soul will be pleased. It is also read as "you will be pleased" (turdā) in the passive form from ardā, meaning: your Lord will please you.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 131:

﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾ i.e., do not prolong your gaze in a manner of desire and inclination ﴿toward that which We have bestowed upon [certain] pairs of them﴾ of the adornments of the world.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿pairs of them﴾ i.e., idols of the disbelievers, "pairs" is the object of "We have bestowed" (matta'na). The prepositional phrase has been placed before it for the sake of giving it emphasis. Alternatively, it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun, and the object is "min-hum" (of them), meaning: toward that which We have bestowed upon them, and it consists of kinds and types of some of them, with the particle "min" understood in the sense of partitiveness (tab'id); or it is "ba'dan minhum" (some of them), with the qualified noun omitted, as has been mentioned many times.

﴿the splendour of the life of this world﴾ is accusative, governed by a verb omitted but indicated by "matta'na" (We have bestowed), meaning: We gave; or it is governed by "bihi" (with it), with its meaning implied (tadmin); or it is in apposition (badaliyya) to the place of "bihi" or to "azwajan" (pairs), with or without a construct phrase being supposed; or it is accusative by way of censure (dhamm), and it is the adornment and the radiance. It has been read as "zahrata" with a fatha on the ha', which is a dialectal form like "al-jahrah" in "al-jahrah" (open declaration); or it is the plural of "zahir" as a description of them, meaning that they are radiant, and "the world" refers to their luxury and the splendour of their appearance, in contrast to the state of the believing ascetics.

﴿that We may test them therein﴾ is connected to "matta'na". It was brought in to warn against it by clarifying its evil outcome in the final destination immediately after showing its splendour in the present state, meaning: that We may deal with them as one who tests and examines them therein; or that We may punish them in the Hereafter on account of it.

﴿And the provision of your Lord﴾ i.e., what has been stored up for you in the Hereafter, or what He has provided you in this world of prophethood and guidance ﴿is better﴾ than what He granted them in this world, because it, in itself, is, together with being the most noble thing that competitors compete for, safe from harm, unlike what they were given.

﴿and more enduring﴾ for its essence or its effect hardly ever ceases, forever, unlike the splendour of this world.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 132:

﴿And enjoin prayer upon your family, and be steadfast in it.﴾ He (ﷺ) was commanded to order his household, or those who followed him among his community, to perform prayer after he himself had been commanded to do so, so that they would help one another in seeking relief from their want, not be preoccupied with the matter of livelihood, and not turn their attention to the attentiveness of the wealthy.

﴿And be steadfast in it﴾: persevere in it, not preoccupied with the matter of making a living.

﴿We do not ask you for provision﴾: that is, We do not burden you to provide sustenance for yourself or your family. ﴿We provide for you﴾ and for them, so empty your heart of concern for the affair of the Hereafter. ﴿And the good end﴾ [i.e., the praiseworthy outcome] ﴿is for righteousness﴾: that is, for the people of righteousness (taqwa), with the omission of the noun (al-mudaf) and the placing of the noun it was annexed to (al-mudaf ilayhi) in its position, drawing attention to the fact that the essence of the matter is taqwa (God-consciousness). It is narrated that when harm befell his household, he (ﷺ) would order them to perform prayer and would recite this verse.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 133:

﴿And they say: "Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?"﴾ This is a report of some of their false statements, which the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to bear patiently. That is, "Why would he not bring us a sign that proves his truthfulness in his claim of prophethood, or a sign of the kind that they proposed?" They reached such a degree of obstinacy and stubbornness that they did not count as signs what they had witnessed of the miracles, before which the solid mountains crumble, and so they dared to utter this monstrous and vile statement.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has there not come to them the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ That is, the Torah, the Gospel, and all the other heavenly books. It is a rejection, from Him, mighty and sublime, of their ugly statement, and a denial of them, in which they concealed beneath it the denial that a sign has come, by pointing to the coming of the noble Qur'an, which is the mother of signs and the foundation of miracles, and the greatest and most enduring of them. This is because the reality of a miracle is that a claimant to prophethood is singled out with some kind of matter that breaks customary norms, whatever that matter may be. There is no doubt that knowledge is the most august and loftiest of matters, since it is the root of deeds and the origin of actions. Indeed, it has appeared, together with its possession of all the sciences of the earlier and later peoples, through the hand of an unlettered man who had not practised any of the sciences and had not studied with anyone from among their people at all. So what miracle is sought after its coming, and what sign is desired in its presence, especially given its introduction under the description of being a clear proof of what is in the former scriptures, the Torah and the Gospel and all the other heavenly books? That is, a witness to the truth of what they contain of the sound beliefs and the foundations of rulings on which all the messengers agreed, and to the correctness of what they state of the reports of the nations. In that it is self-sufficient in its miraculousness from anything that testifies to its truth, it is worthy of establishing the truth of other things, which is no secret, for it highlights its status, illuminates its proof, and further affirms and verifies its coming. Attributing the coming to it, while making them the ones to whom it came, serves to draw attention to its originality in this, together with what it has of appropriateness to the clear proof. The hamza is for denying that it has occurred, and the waw is for conjunction with an implied element that the context requires, as if it were said: "Did not all the other signs come to them, and did not especially the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures come to them?" This is an affirmation of its coming and an announcement that it is so evident that it is not possible for them to deny it at all, even if they dared to deny all the other signs out of obstinacy and stubbornness. It was also read: "أوَلَمْ يَأْتِهِمْ" with the yaa' (ي) of the third person, and it was read: "الصُّحْفِ" with sukun for ease.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 134:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment...﴾ up to the end of the verse, is a resumptive sentence (jumlah musta'nafah) brought to affirm what precedes it, namely that the Qur'an is a clear sign that cannot be denied, by explaining that they will acknowledge it on the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is: If We had destroyed them in this world with a punishment that uproots them ﴿from before it﴾ (min qablihi), which is related to "We destroyed," or to an omitted element that is an attribute of "punishment," i.e., a punishment that existed before the coming of the clear proof, or before Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿they would have said﴾, that is, on the Day of Resurrection:

﴿Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger in the world﴾ with a Book, ﴿so that we might follow Your signs﴾ which he brought to us, ﴿before we were humiliated﴾ by the punishment in the world, ﴿and disgraced﴾ by entering the Fire today. But We did not destroy them before their coming, so their excuse was cut off. At that point they said: ﴿Yes, indeed, a warner came to us, but we denied him and said, "God has not sent down anything."﴾

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 20, verse 135:

﴿Say﴾ to those obstinate disbelievers: ﴿each﴾, that is, each one of us and of you, ﴿is waiting (mutarabbis)﴾, awaiting what our affair and your affair will come to, ﴿so wait (fatarabbasu)﴾. It is also read: "fa-tamatta'u" (so enjoy [what you have]).

﴿Soon you will know﴾ in the near future ﴿who are the companions of the path (al-sirat) that is even (al-sawiyy)﴾, that is, the straight one. It is also read "al-sawa'" (the even), meaning the middle, good course. It is also read "al-su'" and "al-su'a" and "al-suwayy," which is the diminutive of "al-su'" (evil).

﴿And who has been guided (ihtada)﴾ away from misguidance. The "man" (who) in both places is interrogative; its position is nominative by way of the inceptive (mubtada'), its predicate is what follows it, and the clause fills the place of the two objects of "knowing," or of its single object. It is permissible for the second to be a relative pronoun, unlike the first, because there is no returning pronoun; in that case it is coordinated with the place of the interrogative clause whose verb is suspended (mu'allaq), on the basis that "knowing" means "recognizing," or coordinated with "companions" or with "the path." It has also been said: the returning pronoun in the first is omitted, and the estimate is: "Who are the companions of the path?"

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah Ta-Ha, he will be given on the Day of Resurrection the reward of the Emigrants and the Helpers," and he said: "The people of Paradise will recite of the Qur'an only Surah Ta-Ha and Surah Ya-Sin."
